a_rows_sample.anchor: C1. step-001 (140653) -- Operational Independence ... Ind_rho(e_i,e_j,G,C) -> {Independent,Dependent,Unknown} ... section15 the statistical correction: OperationallyIndependent does-not-imply StatisticallyIndependent
a_rows_sample.statement: Step-001 (file 140653) formalizes Operational Independence: Ind_rho(e_i,e_j,G,C) -> {Independent, Dependent, Unknown}, where G is a provenance/dependency graph, C is context, rho is an independence policy; a deterministic rule (a chain relation between two evidence items forces Dependent, 'no LLM required'); a common-ancestor relation implies independence is normally Unknown, not Confirmed; different sources do not imply independence; a six-component independence evidence vector I(e_i,e_j)=(i_S,i_A,i_P,i_M,i_T,i_C) (source/acquisition/provenance/method/temporal independence plus common-ancestor status) each valued in {Confirmed,Rejected,Unknown}, explicitly refusing a scalar IndependenceScore because it 'would obscure why'; states the law 'Independence must be established, not assumed'; and adds a critical statistical correction: operationally-established independence does not imply statistical independence, so Bayesian multiplication's requirement P(E1,E2|H)=P(E1|H)P(E2|H) is a separate, stronger condition -- 'exactly why Evidence Architecture and Statistical Inference Policy must remain separate.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: C2. step-002 (140919) -- Evidence Identity / Equivalence Calculus ... Identity != Semantic Equivalence != Same Observation != Independence. Five relations section5 ... section4 critical invariant: Semantic equivalence must NOT imply deduplication.
a_rows_sample.statement: Step-002 (file 140919) opens with Identity != Semantic Equivalence != Same Observation != Independence and formalizes five relations between evidence items: same-evidence-object (=_I), same-proposition (=_P), same-underlying-observation (=_O), dependency (prec, e2 produced using e1), and operational independence under policy rho (perp_rho); states the critical invariant that semantic equivalence must NOT imply deduplication; works seven cases including 'different values, same observation' yielding a DERIVATION_CONFLICT status distinguishing independent-observation-count from derived-interpretation-count; builds a multi-relational lineage graph G_E=(V,L_1..L_n) with typed edge sets (DerivedFrom, ExtractedFrom, TransformedFrom, SummarizedFrom, CopiedFrom, ObservedFrom, ReviewedFrom); states CommonCause != SameObservation and CommonCause != AutomaticDependence; argues the corpus's eight relationship labels (IDENTICAL, SAME_OBSERVATION, DERIVED, SEMANTICALLY_EQUIVALENT, COMMON_SOURCE, INDEPENDENT, CONTRADICTORY, UNKNOWN) should not collapse into a single enum since they coexist; and distinguishes a fact about provenance from an inference about provenance, warning KnowledgeOS should never silently promote the second into the first.

a_rows_sample.anchor: C3. step-003 (141118) -- Evidence Assessment Algebra ... EA=(S+,S-,U,Q,V,D,X,Pi) ... Notice what is not here: Truth. ... section4 Aggregation must occur after normalization ... section12 not every useful assessment is monotonic
a_rows_sample.statement: Step-003 (file 141118) defines the Evidence Assessment tuple EA=(S+,S-,U,Q,V,D,X,Pi) -- Supporting, Opposing, Uncertainty, Quality, Validity/temporal, Dependency, Context/applicability, Provenance -- explicitly noting Truth is absent from the tuple; refuses S=S+-S- as an aggregate since '0.9 minus 0.8 does not mean 0.1' (there is substantial evidence on both sides); requires aggregation to occur only after a normalization step N_rho handling identity/provenance/semantic/relevance/temporal/dependency/polarity resolution; distinguishes Quality!=Relevance, Reliability!=Validity, ProvenanceQuality!=SourceAuthority; introduces an aggregation equivalence class [e]_~O (same underlying observation aggregated once unless policy states otherwise); and corrects a naive monotonicity claim: not every useful assessment is monotonic -- SupportAggregation may be monotonic with respect to additional supporting evidence while a CompleteAssessment need not be, seeding closure-04a's signed monotonicity and step-004's axiom 6. Establishes the chain Evidence->Assessment->Conclusion->Decision (never Evidence->Decision directly) and four bounded contexts (Evidence/Assessment/Knowledge/Decision Context).

a_rows_sample.anchor: C4. step-004 (142250) -- The Evidence Aggregation Axioms ... Axioms 1-16 ... section19 kernel invariants A1-A4 ... vs policy properties A5-A8. section20 the Evidence Constitution E-K1...E-K10 ... section21 nine-framework comparison table ... There is probably no single universal KnowledgeOS evidence algebra.
a_rows_sample.statement: Step-004 (file 142250) states 16 evidence-aggregation axioms: (1) Determinism (LLM variability != epistemic randomness), (2) permutation invariance, (3) duplicate invariance ('This should be a kernel invariant'), (4) derived-evidence non-inflation, (5) irrelevance invariance, (6) supporting monotonicity with three qualifiers (admissible, independent, supporting evidence) and an explicit disclaimer that it scopes only the S+/S- components, never the final conclusion, (7) contradiction preservation, (8) conflict sensitivity, (9) dependency sensitivity, (10) unknown dependency stays unknown, (11) corroboration (value deliberately left as policy territory), (12) temporal sensitivity (Stale != Delete), (13) context sensitivity ('Evidence has no universal relevance'), (14) provenance preservation, (15) no evidence creation (empty evidence set yields NoEvidence, not 0.5 or Confirmed), (16) no certainty creation (StrongEvidence does not imply Truth). Separates four kernel invariants A1-A4 (identity preservation, provenance preservation, contradiction preservation, no automatic independence) from four policy properties A5-A8 (corroboration rule, saturation, decision threshold, probability interpretation), and states a ten-item Evidence Constitution E-K1..E-K10 covering identity, no-duplicate-inflation, provenance preservation, dependency awareness, unknown-is-not-independent, contradiction preservation, context dependence, Stale!=Deleted, no-truth-by-aggregation, and no-decision-by-aggregation. Compares nine aggregation frameworks (Maximum/Mean/Weighted-sum/Saturating/Bayesian/Dempster-Shafer/Possibility/Argumentation/Graph-based) and concludes there is probably no single universal KnowledgeOS evidence algebra, proposing a fixed kernel plus pluggable assessment calculi C_admissible = {rho | Agg_rho satisfies A_kernel}.

a_rows_sample.anchor: C5. step-005 (142333) -- What Is the Mathematical Object Being Aggregated ... section21 KERNEL/POLICY partition (verbatim sets): KERNEL = {Evidence, Proposition, Provenance, Lineage, Dependency, Context, TemporalValidity, Polarity, AssessmentBasis}; POLICY = {Aggregation, Inference, Thresholds, ProbabilityModels, BeliefModels, DecisionRules}.
a_rows_sample.statement: Step-005 (file 142333) states Evidence != Support != Belief != Probability != Truth, and argues the contribution function c_rho(e,P,C) must deliberately not be typed into [0,1], since '0.8 has no epistemic meaning until its semantics are specified' -- a direct answer to an earlier morning file's problem 4 (094259). Distinguishes seven semantic domains (Reliability, Relevance, Evidential support, Probability, Belief, Plausibility, Information gain) and argues the kernel must not choose one calculus over another. States the single most citable boundary statement in the batch: the KERNEL/POLICY partition, KERNEL = {Evidence, Proposition, Provenance, Lineage, Dependency, Context, TemporalValidity, Polarity, AssessmentBasis} versus POLICY = {Aggregation, Inference, Thresholds, ProbabilityModels, BeliefModels, DecisionRules} -- 'the kernel stores the dimensions, the policy determines how they combine.' Also distinguishes Assessment != Acceptance and EvidenceValue != EvidenceStrength, closing with the verdict 'substantially resolved'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: C6. step-006 (142514) -- Information Gain and Value of Evidence ... Evidence Strength != Information Gain != Decision Value ... section13 q*=argmax U_rho(q|K_t,I_t,P) -- potentially one of the most important equations in the whole KnowledgeOS theory. ... section24 safeguard: refuses Moksha = Delta=0
a_rows_sample.statement: Step-006 (file 142514) distinguishes Evidence Strength != Information Gain != Decision Value; defines information gain IG(e;P)=H(P)-H(P|e) but then explicitly refuses IG=EntropyReduction as a universal law, instead defining a discrepancy-reduction measure IG_D(e), an expected discrepancy reduction EDR(e) made more fundamental than entropy reduction ('KnowledgeOS is trying to move K_t toward I_t, not H(K_t) to 0'), and a value-of-evidence function VOE_rho and utility U_rho(e)=Benefit-Cost with explicitly policy-dependent weights; states q*=argmax_q U_rho(q|K_t,I_t,P) as potentially one of the most important equations in the whole theory; formalizes the guidance triad Zero(K_t,I_t)->Delta_t, Lord(Delta_t)->Q, Sarathi(Q,constraints)->a_t; and provides an explicit safeguard against an earlier morning file's (085756) Moksha-as-maximal-information claim, refusing Moksha=Delta=0 and stating Delta=0 always means only relative to the specified ideal state.

a_rows_sample.anchor: C7. step-007 (142709) -- Knowledge State Transition Algebra ... K_t=(A_t,E_t,R_t,C_t,H_t,Gamma_t) ... section11 eight transition operations O_K ... with a PARTIAL map delta:K x O_K -harpoon-> K ... section33 invariants K1-K8
a_rows_sample.statement: Step-007 (file 142709) defines the Knowledge State tuple K_t=(A_t,E_t,R_t,C_t,H_t,Gamma_t) (Assertions, Evidence, Relations, Conflicts, History, validity conditions), states K_t != H_t and Superseded != Deleted, and mediates Evidence-does-not-imply-Knowledge via an epistemic event rather than evidence directly. Defines eight transition operations O_K = {Introduce, Corroborate, Qualify, Contradict, Supersede, Resolve, Retract, Invalidate} as a PARTIAL function delta:K x O_K -> K (partial because, e.g., Resolve(C) is invalid if C is not an active conflict); states TemporalChange != LogicalContradiction, Retract(A) != Delete(A), Invalidation != Retraction; rejects a single linear lifecycle in favor of a multidimensional epistemic-state vector Sigma_A=(Acquisition,Support,Uncertainty,Validity); models event sourcing K_t=Fold(delta,H_t,K_0) and K_t=F(K_0,H_t,rho,omega) with rho=policy version and omega=ontology/model version; states Knowledge-time != Source-time != Validity-time; takes a paraconsistent stance allowing P and not-P representable without trivializing the whole state; and closes with eight invariants K1-K8 (Evidence does not imply Accepted Knowledge; Superseded/Retracted != Deleted; P and not-P coexist without collapse; three distinct time coordinates; reconstructibility; policy versioning; semantic versioning; state-transition function). Leaves deliberately unresolved: 'when exactly is a conclusion allowed to modify the Knowledge State?' -- handed to step-008.

a_rows_sample.anchor: D2. step-025a-1 (181325) ... Honesty flag, verbatim: I attempted to execute the first prototype ... the execution environment did not successfully complete the run. So I will not claim experimental results that I have not actually obtained. ... section6 [UNRESOLVED] EVIDENCE FLAG
a_rows_sample.statement: Step-025a-1 (file 181325) opens with an honesty flag: an attempted first prototype execution did not successfully complete, so the author explicitly declines to claim unobtained experimental results. Defines nine fundamental types (WorldState W_t != K_t; Observation O; Evidence E, explicitly Observation != Evidence; Assertion A; Assessment Q(A,E,C); KnowledgeState K_t=(A_t,Q_t,E_t,C_t,P_t); Goal G, Goal != Action; Knowledge Requirement R; Epistemic Contract C_G) and a minimal state K_t=(E_t,A_t,Q_t,C_t,P_t,V_t) with G and C_G kept outside it, marked PROVISIONAL. Raises an explicit [UNRESOLVED] question -- whether evidence is actually part of K_t or merely externally referenced -- refusing to resolve it by intuition and instead proposing to test which representation is required for historical reconstruction, retraction, provenance, and conflict resolution. Runs eight attack scenarios including the discovery that more knowledge can increase |K_{t+1}| while decreasing Readiness(K_{t+1}), and that Authorization=False implies Execute=Forbidden as part of state-transition semantics, not merely policy overlay.

a_rows_sample.anchor: D6. step-025a-5 (182235) -- Property-Based Falsification ... I1-I14 results ... Two genuine threats section21: CircularDependencies and EvidenceIdentity. ... section28 emergent structure: K=(V,E,R,T,P,D,M) ... governed temporal epistemic graph
a_rows_sample.statement: Step-025a-5 (file 182235) property-tests the ten invariants I1-I10 (originating in step-025a-4) plus four newly promoted invariants I11-I14 (I11 No hindsight: a decision's basis is the knowledge state at decision time, not the current one; I12 World/knowledge independence; I13 Revision must not imply falsehood -- invalidating the only supporting evidence yields Unknown, not False; I14 Conflict resolution must preserve history) against generated adversarial sequences, all fourteen passing with qualifications; identifies exactly two genuine unresolved threats -- CircularDependencies (a derivation cycle A1 supports A2 and A2 supports A1, with AcyclicDerivationGraph proposed but not established) and EvidenceIdentity (not reducible to a text hash) -- plus four further threats (scale/propagation cost, stale rules requiring RuleVersion, changing ontology entering epistemic lineage, and source authority requiring temporal semantics with Truth != Authority); proposes the emergent structure K=(V,E,R,T,P,D,M) (epistemic objects, evidence/support relations, assessments/rules, temporal semantics, provenance, dependency/derivation, model/ontology/rule versions), characterizing KnowledgeOS as an increasingly revealed 'governed temporal epistemic graph' -- marked a strong emerging architectural result; and includes an explicit integrity disclaimer that no automated property-based software test was actually executed, only a conceptual/adversarial falsification pass.

a_rows_sample.anchor: D7. step-025b (182411) -- Adversarial End-to-End Simulation ... section13 the demonstrated result: after the restore test, KnowledgeGain>0 but MigrationReadiness down => KnowledgeGain != ProgressTowardGoal ... 025b is the file that generates the entire 025C-025G research agenda
a_rows_sample.statement: Step-025b (file 182411) runs a full end-to-end adversarial simulation (a Nexus migration scenario) covering the whole epistemic-to-operational loop rather than just the kernel, defining an epistemic contract EC_G with nine named requirements and stating Goal != EpistemicContract and Input != Evidence; demonstrates, inside the simulated loop rather than merely arguing it, that after a restore test KnowledgeGain > 0 while MigrationReadiness simultaneously decreases, establishing KnowledgeGain != ProgressTowardGoal empirically within the scenario; formalizes Delta = Zero(K_t, I, EC_G) decomposed into Epistemic/Operational/Governance gaps; states Lord does not necessarily change the world (it may select an epistemic action first); defines the pipeline Recommendation -> Decision -> Authorization -> Execution; runs five injected attacks (LLM hallucination, conflicting sources, stale source, changed requirement, execution failure becoming new evidence); defines six epistemic stopping conditions S1-S6 and an epistemic budget B_epi = {Time, Cost, Risk, HumanAttention, Compute}; distinguishes the epistemic loop from the operational loop; and closes by generating the entire subsequent research agenda (unresolved items U1-U6 feeding directly into steps 025c, 025c-3, 025d, 025f, 025g).

a_rows_sample.anchor: TV-F-020 -- The dependency relation prec has inconsistent orientation at its birth site ... step-002 section5 defines e1 prec e2 as "e2 was produced using e1" (parent prec child). Step-002 section6 Case B ... then writes e2 prec e1 -- child prec parent -- with the author's own caveat "depending on how we orient the provenance relation."
a_rows_sample.statement: TV-F-020 finds, by direct comparison of the definition site and first-use site within the same source file, that step-002's dependency relation e1 prec e2 (defined in section 5 as 'e2 was produced using e1', parent-to-child) is used with the opposite orientation (e2 prec e1, child-to-parent) in section 6's Case B, with the author's own caveat acknowledging the orientation is undecided ('depending on how we orient the provenance relation'). Classifies this as UNDER-SPECIFIED, not a mathematical error, since both orientations give isomorphic theory, but notes every formal statement using prec downstream (step-004's E-K4, step-003's dependency sensitivity) silently assumes the section-5 orientation, and a candidate kernel document (K0's P5 frame) adopted that orientation only as a PROPOSED RECONSTRUCTION -- the source itself never settles it. Neither file cites or maps to the other's alphabet ... this finding pins the origin of the transition-alphabet divergence to 007->009, before any later fork.
a_rows_sample.statement: TV-F-021 finds two partially overlapping, mutually silent transition-operation alphabets defined over the same carrier K within a single day: step-007's 8-operation O_K = {Introduce, Corroborate, Qualify, Contradict, Supersede, Resolve, Retract, Invalidate} (with delta: K x O_K -> K) and step-009's 9-operation R_K = {Contextualize, Corroborate, Downgrade, Retract, Supersede, Accept, Reject, Defer, Resolve} (with Revise: K x R_K -> K), sharing exactly four operations (Corroborate, Retract, Supersede, Resolve) while diverging on the rest, with neither file citing or mapping to the other and step-009 never stating whether R_K extends, replaces, or coexists with O_K. Therefore Zero != simple sub
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the naive Delta=Target-Current model of Zero using a four-requirement worked example (known/unknown/conflicting/missing), establishing Zero≠simple subtraction — it must compare requirements against epistemic state.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Let the goal be G. The goal induces a set of required knowledge conditions: R_G={r_1,r_2,...,r_n}. For Nexus migration ... r_1=CurrentVersionKnown ... r_7=GovernanceApprovalObtained. This is crucial: Zero cannot be computed from the goal alone. We need the Epistemic Contract that tells us what must
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the Knowledge Requirement set R_G induced by a goal G (worked with seven Nexus-migration requirements r1-r7), establishing that Zero cannot be computed from the goal alone and requires an Epistemic Contract.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Define EC_G=(R_G,Gamma_G) where R_G = required conditions; Gamma_G = rules determining sufficiency. So EC_G = what must be established + how sufficiency is judged. This gives Zero a formal input.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the Epistemic Contract EC_G=(R_G,Γ_G) — required conditions plus sufficiency rules — as Zero's formal input.

b_rows_sample.anchor: For each requirement r_i, we evaluate its status against K_t. Define Sat(K_t,r_i). Initially I propose the following state set: S={Satisfied, PartiallySatisfied, Unknown, Insufficient, Conflicted, Stale, Invalid, Prohibited, NotApplicable}. This is already much richer than Boolean logic.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a nine-value requirement-satisfaction status set (Satisfied, PartiallySatisfied, Unknown, Insufficient, Conflicted, Stale, Invalid, Prohibited, NotApplicable), explicitly richer than Boolean logic.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose Sat(K,r)=False. That could mean: we know it is false; we don't know; evidence conflicts; evidence is stale; evidence was invalidated; governance prohibits the action. These are operationally very different. Therefore Sat != Boolean.
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues Sat≠Boolean: a bare False collapses six operationally distinct situations (known-false, unknown, conflicting, stale, invalidated, prohibited) into one indistinguishable value.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We can define Z_i=Status(K_t,r_i,EC_G). Then Zero(K_t,G,EC_G)={(r_i,Z_i) | r_i in R_G}. This gives us a Zero vector. For example Z(K)=[Satisfied,Satisfied,Unknown,Insufficient,Conflicted,Satisfied,Missing]. Now Zero is computationally representable.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Zero(K_t,G,EC_G)={(r_i,Z_i)} as a computationally representable 'Zero vector' of per-requirement statuses.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Case A: No evidence exists: Evidence(r)=empty. Status: Unknown. Case B: Governance requires approval, and no approval exists. That is Missing. These are different. So I recommend Missing as a separate status where the requirement itself is an expected governed artifact/action.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Unknown (no evidence exists at all) from Missing (an expected governed artifact/action, such as an approval, that does not exist) as two different status values.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose current KnowledgeState contains A_1: NexusVersion=3.69, A_2: RepositoryCount=43, but nothing about rollback. Then Status(r_1)=Satisfied but Status(r_3)=Unknown. If Architecture Board approval is explicitly required and has not been issued: Status(r_7)=Missing. Therefore Zero(K)={r_3:Unknown,
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked Nexus example computing a concrete Zero(K)={r3:Unknown, r7:Missing} from partial knowledge state evidence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We can therefore define Zero(K,G,EC)=R_G \ Satisfied(K,R_G) but this is only a shorthand. The real result must retain why each requirement is not satisfied. So Zero={Requirement, Status, Evidence, Reason, Dependencies}.
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects a shorthand set-difference definition of Zero (R_G minus satisfied requirements) into the fuller structured form Zero={Requirement,Status,Evidence,Reason,Dependencies}, retaining why each requirement is unsatisfied.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A Zero item should look conceptually like: Requirement: RollbackVerified; Status: Unknown; SupportingEvidence: none; BlockingReason: no successful restore test; RequiredAction: perform restore test; DecisionCriticality: high. This is already implementable.
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives a concrete implementable structured-Zero-item template with six fields (Requirement, Status, SupportingEvidence, BlockingReason, RequiredAction, DecisionCriticality).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose E_1 supports RollbackVerified=True. Is that enough? Not necessarily. The epistemic contract may require 2 independent tests. Or 1 test witnessed by a designated authority. Or Probability(success)>=0.99. Therefore Satisfied = ContractSpecific.
b_rows_sample.statement: Establishes that satisfaction of a requirement is ContractSpecific — the same supporting evidence may or may not count as satisfied depending on the epistemic contract's own sufficiency rule (independent-test count, witness authority, or probability threshold).

b_rows_sample.anchor: We therefore need Satisfied(K,r,EC) which may invoke the appropriate reasoning model. For example Satisfied(K,r,EC)=RuleEngine(K,r,EC) or =StatisticalCriterion(K,r,EC) or =HumanAuthorization(K,r). This is another reason Zero must not contain one universal inference mechanism.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the satisfaction predicate Satisfied(K,r,EC) as potentially delegating to RuleEngine, StatisticalCriterion, or HumanAuthorization — reinforcing that Zero must not embed one universal inference mechanism.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero should not calculate everything itself. Instead: Zero -> RequirementEvaluation -> AppropriateReasoningModel. ... Zero aggregates the results.
b_rows_sample.statement: Establishes Zero as an orchestrator that dispatches requirement evaluation to the appropriate reasoning model (Rules/Statistics/Authority) and aggregates results, rather than being an inference engine itself.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Operational Zero: Z_W=Distance(W_t,W*) where W* is the target world state. Epistemic Zero: Z_K=Distance(K_t,K*_EC) where K*_EC is the knowledge required by the epistemic contract. These are fundamentally different.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formally splits Operational Zero Z_W=Distance(W_t,W*) from Epistemic Zero Z_K=Distance(K_t,K*_EC), reaffirming the two are fundamentally different quantities.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Target: Nexus Pro running in target environment. Current world: Nexus OSS 3.69 running. Operational gap: Z_W>0. But suppose Target architecture known, Current version known, Backup status unknown, Firewall status unknown, Approval missing. Then Z_K>0. Even if an engineer knows exactly how to perform
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example showing Z_K (epistemic gap) can independently block execution even when the operational how-to is fully known, illustrating Z_W and Z_K as genuinely separate blocking gaps.

b_rows_sample.anchor: I recommend Zero=(Z_world, Z_knowledge, Z_governance, Z_decision) at the conceptual level. Z_world: What differs in reality? Z_knowledge: What required facts are unknown/uncertain? Z_governance: What required approvals/rules are missing? Z_decision: What prevents a defensible decision? This is much
b_rows_sample.statement: Decomposes Zero into four conceptual dimensions (Z_world, Z_knowledge, Z_governance, Z_decision), each answering a distinct question, stronger than a single scalar distance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose Z_knowledge=5 and Z_governance=1. Can we say Zero=6? No. The six missing items are not necessarily comparable. One missing governance approval could be more blocking than five low-priority informational gaps. Therefore Zero is primarily a structured object, not a scalar.
b_rows_sample.statement: Counterexample against summing dimension counts into a scalar Zero=6: a single governance gap can outweigh five informational gaps in blocking severity, so Zero must remain primarily a structured object, not a scalar.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Once the structured Zero exists, we may calculate: GapCount. Or CriticalGapCount. Or WeightedGapScore. Or ContractCoverage. For example Coverage(K) = satisfied required conditions / total required conditions. But these are projections of Zero, not Zero itself.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines four derivable scalar projections of the structured Zero object (GapCount, CriticalGapCount, WeightedGapScore, ContractCoverage), explicitly distinguished as projections, not Zero itself.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Each requirement can have Criticality(r) such as {Critical,High,Medium,Low}. But again, we should be careful with arbitrary scores. A critical requirement might be RollbackVerified. If Status=Unknown, then migration could be blocked regardless of all other results. This gives us BlockingCondition.
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces per-requirement Criticality with a caution against arbitrary scoring, deriving the concept of a BlockingCondition — a single unresolved critical requirement that blocks regardless of all other results.

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels co-occur in the same contribution's labels[] 2 separate times across the corpus

a_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal O,\mathcal E,\mathcal A,\mathcal M,\mathcal C,\mathcal D,\mathcal X,\mathcal V,\mathcal F ... are different types. We must not treat everything as a generic knowledge item
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a typed mathematical universe of nine explicitly disjoint object sets (Observations, Evidence, Assertions, Models, Constraints, Decisions, Actions, Validation results, Conflicts).

a_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal I for identities/entities ... \mathcal B bounded contexts (b_{infra},b_{architecture},b_{governance},b_{security}) ... Meaning(x,b)
a_rows_sample.statement: Adds entity/identity space I and bounded-context space B, giving context-relative Meaning(x,b).

a_rows_sample.anchor: a=(i,p,v,b,\tau,\sigma) ... prevents version=3.70 from being treated as merely an arbitrary string
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes an assertion as a six-tuple with a predicate-dependent value domain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: e=(id,source,content,observedAt,acquiredAt,context,provenance) ... Supports(e,a)
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes evidence as a seven-field tuple with a Supports(e,a) relation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Supports(e,a)\not\Rightarrow True(a). Instead Supports(e,a)\rightarrow JustificationContribution(e,a)
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes the evidence/truth distinction as a mathematical relation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Derives(X,a) ... \{e_1,e_2,c_1\}\vdash a ... different from saying the conclusion is objectively true
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines derivability via a turnstile relation, distinct from objective truth.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_t=(E_t,A_t,M_t,C_t,F_t,V_t,R_t) ... one of the most important formalizations so far
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes Knowledge State as a seven-component tuple.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_t\xrightarrow{event}K_{t+1} ... \delta:K\times Event\rightarrow K ... a formal state-transition system
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a formal event-driven state-transition function delta.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ObservationAdded, AssertionDerived, EvidenceInvalidated, ValidationCompleted, ConstraintChanged ... knowledge evolution is event-driven, not destructive mutation
a_rows_sample.statement: Lists five example event types, restating event-driven, non-destructive knowledge evolution.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_t=Fold(e_1,\ldots,e_t) ... KnowledgeState=Projection(EventHistory) ... a mathematically clean basis for event sourcing
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes current knowledge as a projection of historical events.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Consistent(K_t)=C_L\land C_T\land C_S\land C_P\land C_D\land C_C ... much more informative than one score
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally decomposes Consistent(K_t) into a six-way conjunction of consistency dimensions, resolving a gap flagged in S0924.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Consistent(K)=True ... must not be conflated with True(K) ... Consistent(K)=True while Reality\not\models K ... preserves Step 30
a_rows_sample.statement: States the important correction that formal consistency must never be conflated with world-truth.

a_rows_sample.anchor: W_t ... Obs(W_t)=O_t ... knowledge is constructed from O_t rather than directly from W_t
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes partial observational access to the real world state.

a_rows_sample.anchor: \Omega:W\rightarrow O ... W\xrightarrow{\Omega}O\xrightarrow{f}K
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines the observation function and composed observation-to-knowledge pipeline.

a_rows_sample.anchor: \Omega(W_1)=\Omega(W_2) while W_1\neq W_2 ... No algorithm can recover information that the observation function destroys ... an information-theoretic limitation
a_rows_sample.statement: States a formal impossibility result explicitly framed as information-theoretic, not an AI limitation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Identifiability(g,\Omega) ... one of the strongest mathematical foundations of the whole architecture
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines identifiability, called one of the strongest mathematical foundations of the architecture.

a_rows_sample.anchor: g is not identifiable from current observations ... KnowledgeOS must therefore be allowed to return Underdetermined
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines the Underdetermined result required for non-identifiable properties.

a_rows_sample.anchor: q=(H,P,Model,Context,Time,Evidence) ... requires a probability model; a reference context; assumptions; evidence
a_rows_sample.statement: Types a probability object with six required components.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Unknown(H) rather than P(H)=0.5 ... a type distinction, not merely a numerical convention
a_rows_sample.statement: States Unknown(H) must be a distinct type, not merely a numerical convention.

a_rows_sample.anchor: U(H)=(type,value,model,scope,source) ... type\in\{Probability,Interval,SetValued,Unknown,Qualitative\} ... more flexible than forcing every assertion into a probability
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a five-field, five-typed Uncertainty object.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Can KnowledgeOS compute K_{t+1} from K_t and new evidence? ... K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,E_t,\Omega,EC)
b_rows_sample.statement: States the central question of the step and defines the fundamental transition function K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,E_t,Omega,EC) where K_t=current state, E_t=new epistemic input, Omega=domain ontology/rules, EC=applicable epistemic contract.

type_signature.domain: KnowledgeState x EpistemicInput x Ontology x EpistemicContract

b_rows_sample.anchor: K=(Assertions,Evidence,Provenance,Relations,Assessments,Validity,TemporalState,Conflicts,Versions,Contracts,Policies)
b_rows_sample.statement: Rejects K={facts} in favor of an 11-component tuple K=(Assertions, Evidence, Provenance, Relations, Assessments, Validity, TemporalState, Conflicts, Versions, Contracts, Policies), with Decisions/Actions/Observations optionally included depending on whether event history is treated as part of state or an external log.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeState=DerivedState ... EventLog=HistoricalCause ... an important DDD distinction
b_rows_sample.statement: Recommends keeping the event log conceptually separate from the derived KnowledgeState: Events_t and K_t=Fold(Events_0..t), giving KnowledgeState=DerivedState vs EventLog=HistoricalCause — 'an important DDD distinction.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: 10:00 Nexus=3.69, 11:00 Nexus=3.70, 12:00 Nexus=3.70 ... CurrentKnowledge\neq HistoricalKnowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: a three-event history where the current state (3.70) differs from the full history (3.69->3.70), showing both are valuable — CurrentKnowledge ≠ HistoricalKnowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: DeterministicUpdate ... our first major invariant
b_rows_sample.statement: States the first invariant: for fixed (K_t,E_t,Omega,EC), Update must produce the same K_{t+1} on repeated execution — DeterministicUpdate.

b_rows_sample.anchor: RawInput\rightarrow LLM\rightarrow CandidateEvidence ... NonDeterministicAcquisition\rightarrow GovernedInput\rightarrow DeterministicStateTransition
b_rows_sample.statement: Resolves the LLM-nondeterminism concern: an LLM may participate before admission (RawInput->LLM->CandidateEvidence), but once admitted as a structured event E_t the transition is deterministic — 'one of the most important architectural boundaries we have discovered.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Update(Update(K,E),E)\equiv Update(K,E) ... idempotence
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the second invariant, idempotence: applying the same evidence twice should not create artificial additional knowledge, Update(Update(K,E),E) ≡ Update(K,E), worked with a duplicate-database-record example resolved via EvidenceID(E1)=EvidenceID(E2) duplicate detection.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Update must never destroy the source lineage ... Provenance(K)\supseteq Provenance(E)
b_rows_sample.statement: States the third invariant, provenance preservation: after E->A->K, Provenance(K) ⊇ Provenance(E) — 'Update must be provenance-preserving.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: UnresolvedConflict\rightarrow UnresolvedConflict unless new evidence or governance explicitly resolves it
b_rows_sample.statement: States the fourth invariant, contradiction preservation: contradictory same-time/context evidence with no resolution rule must remain an unresolved conflict rather than being silently resolved.

b_rows_sample.anchor: NoImplicitConflictResolution ... must not create A or B as the uniquely accepted truth merely because one looks more likely
b_rows_sample.statement: States the fifth invariant, no hallucinated resolution: given A⊥B with no authorized resolution rule, Update must not pick a winner because it 'looks more likely' — NoImplicitConflictResolution.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K_t\subseteq K_{t+1} ... not always true ... naive monotonicity fails
b_rows_sample.statement: Tests naive monotonicity (K_t⊆K_{t+1}) against a version-change example (3.69->3.70 changes current state) and finds it fails.

b_rows_sample.anchor: H_t\subseteq H_{t+1} ... History is monotonic; CurrentState need not be
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines the sixth invariant into event-sourced monotonicity: historical event knowledge H_t is monotonic (events accumulate, history is never erased) even though current derived state is not — 'History is monotonic; CurrentState need not be' — 'a much better formulation.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: H_{t+1}=H_t\cup\{E_t\} ... K_{t+1}=Derive(H_{t+1},\Omega,EC) ... elegant
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes the two-layer transition: H_{t+1}=H_t ∪ {E_t} (monotonic history growth) then K_{t+1}=Derive(H_{t+1},Omega,EC) (current state recomputation) — 'elegant.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Retract(E_1) ... Status(E_1)=Retracted ... K_{current} is recalculated
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines retraction: a source's later 'the previous record was incorrect' becomes Retract(E1), setting Status(E1)=Retracted (not deleting E1 from history), then recalculating K_current.

b_rows_sample.anchor: E_2:Correction(E_1,3.69) ... preserve E_1 and record E_2 ... Correction\neq Deletion
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines correction as distinct from retraction/deletion: E2=Correction(E1,3.69) preserves E1 while recording the correcting event E2; the derived state may change to 3.69 — 'Correction ≠ Deletion.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: The certificate used to establish the evidence has been revoked ... EvidenceValidity(E)=False ... Assertion separate from EvidenceAssessment
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines revocation: a source can become invalid (e.g. a revoked certificate) without the proposition itself being false, EvidenceValidity(E)=False while the assertion remains historically recorded — demonstrates Assertion must be kept separate from EvidenceAssessment.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ValidFrom\le t<ValidUntil ... Expired\neq False
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines explicit validity intervals; when t>=ValidUntil the knowledge becomes Expired, explicitly distinct from False — 'this distinction is extremely important.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: True/Supported, False/Refuted, Unknown, Expired, Conflicted ... must not be collapsed into a single Boolean
b_rows_sample.statement: Lists (at least) five epistemic states that must not be collapsed into a single Boolean: Supported, Refuted, Unknown, Expired, and potentially Conflicted.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal E=\{Unknown,Supported,Refuted,Conflicted,Expired,Retracted\} ... I would not yet call this a simple lattice ... Expired does not necessarily mean Refuted
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a six-state epistemic space E={Unknown,Supported,Refuted,Conflicted,Expired,Retracted} but explicitly declines to call it a simple lattice since some states are orthogonal dimensions (Expired does not imply Refuted; Retracted may concern evidence rather than assertion).

b_rows_sample.anchor: EpistemicState=(SupportStatus,ValidityStatus,ConflictStatus,TemporalStatus) ... much more expressive
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines the epistemic-state space into a four-dimension tuple EpistemicState=(SupportStatus,ValidityStatus,ConflictStatus,TemporalStatus), worked with two example instantiations (one with ConflictStatus=none, one with ConflictStatus=conflicted) — 'much more expressive.'

a_aliases: Mathematical Formalization and Consistency Audit of KnowledgeOS

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'formal-epistemic-type-system-audit-algebra' POSSIBLY relates to 'knowledge-state-closure-algebra' (batch B0022). Note: S0925's Step 31: the first fully executed formal-type-system audit of the whole KnowledgeOS theory (typed universe, formal Knowledge State, partial composition functions, epistemic type safety, twenty counterexamples); synthesizes and formally re-derives many earlier objects (knowledge-state-closure-algebra, model-boundary-observability-identifiability-algebra, uncertainty-calculus-multidimensional-algebra) into one audited formal system.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Given everything currently known, what should happen next? ... Lord(K_t,Z_t,G,C)\rightarrow a_t
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Lord's fundamental operator: Lord(K_t, Z_t=Zero(K_t,EC), G, C) -> a_t, the next action; framed as needing to answer 'given everything currently known, what should happen next?' without letting Lord become 'an uncontrolled LLM planner.'

type_signature.domain: KnowledgeState x ZeroResult x Goal x Constraints

a_rows_sample.anchor: Action=EpistemicAction\cup OperationalAction
a_rows_sample.statement: Separates two action categories: Epistemic action q: K_t -> K_{t+1} (e.g. query database, inspect configuration, search documentation, ask human, run test, verify firewall, compare documents) and Operational action a: W_t -> W_{t+1} (e.g. deploy, migrate, restart, modify configuration, create infrastructure); Action = EpistemicAction ∪ OperationalAction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Lord selects; Governance authorizes; Executor executes ... much safer than LLM\rightarrow Shell
a_rows_sample.statement: Lord proposes a CandidateAction; a governed execution layer separately checks Authorized?/Safe?/ContractSatisfied?/Allowed?; therefore 'Lord selects; Governance authorizes; Executor executes,' explicitly contrasted as much safer than a direct LLM -> Shell architecture.

a_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal A(K_t) ... Lord cannot choose an action outside \mathcal A
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a bounded candidate action space A(K_t) (e.g. {QueryFirewall, InspectBackup, AskArchitect, RunRestoreTest, MigrateNexus, DoNothing}); Lord cannot choose an action outside this set.

a_rows_sample.anchor: a^*=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal A} VOI(a) ... insufficient
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects a naive first formulation a*=argmax_a VOI(a) as insufficient because VOI captures only information/decision value and ignores authorization, safety, cost, urgency, dependencies, and reversibility.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A=(Purpose,ExpectedGain,Cost,Risk,Urgency,Reversibility,Authorization,Dependencies,Deadline) ... resist prematurely creating Score(A)=0.83
a_rows_sample.statement: Represents an action as a nine-dimensional vector A=(Purpose, ExpectedGain, Cost, Risk, Urgency, Reversibility, Authorization, Dependencies, Deadline), explicitly warning against prematurely collapsing it to a scalar Score(A)=0.83 which 'would hide semantics.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Feasible(a,K_t,C) ... RunRestoreTest ... Feasible=True ... MigrateNexus RollbackVerified=unknown ... Feasible=False
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Feasible(a,K_t,C), worked with two examples: RunRestoreTest is Feasible=True (all preconditions available/acceptable), while MigrateNexus is Feasible=False when RollbackVerified=unknown is a blocking condition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A_{feasible}=\{a\in A\mid Feasible(a,K,C)\} ... a^*=Select(A_{feasible},Objective)
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes the two-stage algorithm: first compute A_feasible = {a in A | Feasible(a,K,C)}, then a* = Select(A_feasible, Objective); Lord's two responsibilities are therefore (1) remove impossible/unauthorized actions, (2) choose among the remaining — 'Feasibility -> Optimization.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Zero={RollbackUnknown, FirewallConflicted, ApprovalMissing} ... ApprovalMissing is a hard governance blocker ... MigrateNexus is infeasible
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: given three concurrent Zero gaps and four candidate actions (run restore test, query firewall, ask Architecture Board, execute migration), a hard governance blocker (ApprovalMissing) renders MigrateNexus infeasible, so Lord must choose among the information/governance actions instead.

a_rows_sample.anchor: RootGap(Z)=r_1 ... Lord should not necessarily target r_3. It should target the root gap
a_rows_sample.statement: Root-gap analysis reusing the dependency chain r1=BackupExists -> r2=RestoreValidated -> r3=RollbackVerified: if r3=Unknown is caused by r1=Unknown, Lord should target RootGap(Z)=r1, not r3 — described as 'graph reasoning, not LLM intuition,' making Lord 'more efficient.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: BackupExists -> RestoreEnvironmentAvailable -> RestoreTest -> RollbackVerified -> MigrationEligible
a_rows_sample.statement: Depicts the action dependency graph Lord can traverse to reach the root-gap-resolving action.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,E_q) ... VOI(q) ... depends on a model ... ExpectedOutcomeModel(q)
a_rows_sample.statement: For an epistemic action q, defines K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,E_q) and states VOI(q) requires access to an ExpectedOutcomeModel(q), reiterating that VOI depends on a model (as established in the prior evidence/VOI thread).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Outcome(q)=\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\} with probabilities or qualitative likelihoods where appropriate
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes expected from guaranteed outcomes: querying a database has an expected result (record found) but may fail; Outcome(q) is a set of possible outcomes with probabilities or qualitative likelihoods, letting Lord evaluate expected consequences.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EU(q)=\sum_e P(e\mid q,K)\max_a EU(a\mid K,e) ... VOI(q)=EU(q)-EU(a^*) ... optional specialized engine, not part of the epistemic kernel
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives the classical statistical/decision-theoretic version: EU(q)=sum_e P(e|q,K) max_a EU(a|K,e); VOI(q)=EU(q)-EU(a*); explicitly classified as 'an optional specialized engine, not part of the epistemic kernel.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: HighValue>MediumValue>LowValue ... q_1\succeq q_2 ... KnowledgeOS should not manufacture probabilities
a_rows_sample.statement: Where probabilities are unavailable, proposes a qualitative ordering (HighValue > MediumValue > LowValue) or a partial preference relation q1 ⪰ q2, motivated by the principle that 'KnowledgeOS should not manufacture probabilities.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: q_1: resolve governance blocker ... q_2: collect additional architecture detail ... q_1\succ q_2 ... No numerical score is needed
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example showing a qualitative preference (q1 directly unblocks the goal, q2 does not, so q1 ≻ q2) can be established without any numerical score — 'preferable when quantitative utility is unavailable.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Prefer(a_1,a_2\mid K,G,C) ... rather than assuming Score(a) ... a_1\succ a_2, a_2\succ a_1, or a_1\sim a_2
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes Lord's decision relation Prefer(a1,a2|K,G,C) with outcomes {a1≻a2, a2≻a1, a1~a2} rather than assuming a scalar Score(a); a1~a2 means 'both are equally defensible under current knowledge.'

type_signature.domain: Action x Action x KnowledgeState x Goal x Constraints

a_rows_sample.anchor: IndeterminatePreference\rightarrow HumanDecision ... rather than arbitrary AI selection
a_rows_sample.statement: When a1~a2 and the system cannot distinguish them by governed criteria, Lord may ask for human preference: IndeterminatePreference -> HumanDecision, rather than arbitrary AI selection.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Safety(a,K,C) must hold ... RollbackVerified=Unknown ... Safety=False ... MigrateNexus\notin A_{feasible}
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Safety(a,K,C) as a required precondition before selecting an operational action; e.g. ProductionMigration requiring RollbackVerified=True fails Safety when RollbackVerified=Unknown, excluding MigrateNexus from A_feasible.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Authorized(a,C) must be true ... rm -rf ... Authorized=False ... Capability\neq Authority
a_rows_sample.statement: An AI may be technically capable of an action (e.g. 'rm -rf ...') yet Authorized(a,C)=False makes it non-candidate: 'Capability ≠ Authority' — 'a fundamental separation.'

b_rows_sample.statement: Step-025g (file 183746) formalizes Lord(K_t,Z_t,G,C) -> a_t, splitting Action into EpistemicAction (q: K_t -> K_{t+1}) and OperationalAction (a: W_t -> W_{t+1}) under the rule 'Lord selects; Governance authorizes; Executor executes'; rejects a^*=argmax VOI(a) as insufficient and instead defines a nine-dimension action utility vector A=(Purpose,ExpectedGain,Cost,Risk,Urgency,Reversibility,Authorization,Dependencies,Deadline), explicitly refusing a collapsed scalar Score(A) that 'would hide semantics'; uses a two-stage feasibility-then-optimization algorithm and root-gap analysis (graph reasoning, not LLM intuition); offers an optional statistical expected-utility engine but favors a qualitative preference relation Prefer(a1,a2|K,G,C) (deliberately arg-prefer, not arg-max-Score, 'we have not yet established that these dimensions can legitimately be collapsed'); states Capability != Authority; states the default Lord policy verbatim ('prefer the least risky authorized action that maximally reduces decision-critical Zero, subject to cost, dependencies and deadlines'); defines a termination algebra {Completed,Blocked,Escalated,Abandoned,Expired} with DoNothing in ActionSpace and 'no action is preferable to an unjustified action'; runs five experiments and six falsification passes, including the finding that high information value cannot override governance and that an LLM recommendation cannot override Zero/Contract; and commissions Sarathi (step-025H) as the next research item, delivered the following day outside this batch.

Zero is primarily a structured object, not a scalar"). This is the sharpest intra-band contradiction (VA-2).
b_rows_sample.statement: Identifies the sharpest intra-band contradiction (VA-2): step-025g's action-selection operator a* = arg-prefer over a six-dimensional codomain (GapReduction, Safety, Authorization, Cost, Urgency, Reversibility) is not a well-defined operator -- no order, lexicographic priority, Pareto rule, or aggregation is given, which the source itself concedes ('we have not yet established that these dimensions can legitimately be collapsed'); yet the very next section's worked ranking step implicitly counts gaps (GapReduction(a3) > GapReduction(a1) because a3 closes two gaps versus one), directly contradicting step-025d's own explicit claim that gaps 'are not necessarily comparable' and that 'Zero is primarily a structured object, not a scalar.' b_rows_sample.anchor: Global invariant I_global(S); reachable-states quantification; safety versus liveness
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a global invariant I_global(S) required for every valid system state S, with the architectural objective for-all S in ReachableStates: I_global(S)=True (not every imaginable state, only validly reachable ones, via Reach(KOS,S_0)). Distinguishes Safety ('something bad never happens', e.g. UnauthorizedAction ⇒ not-Executed) from Liveness ('something good eventually happens', e.g. SubmittedRevision ⇒ Eventually(ProcessedRevision)); a system that never decides is safe but useless, so Safety alone is insufficient -- KnowledgeOS needs Safety + Liveness + EpistemicIntegrity + Traceability.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Error propagation versus containment; fail-safe is not universally fail-closed; risk-weighted assurance
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes errors that must propagate (CriticalEvidenceInvalid -> DecisionReevaluation) from errors that should be contained (MalformedOptionalMetadata -> RejectMetadata), requiring explicit error semantics. For critical authorization, Unknown -> Block may be appropriate; for noncritical informational features, Unknown -> ContinueWithWarning may be acceptable, so FailurePolicy is part of the domain/governance contract -- fail-safe is not universally 'fail closed': a global AllFailures -> Block rule would make the system impractical; correct behavior depends on Risk and DecisionType. Formalizes risk-weighted assurance AssuranceRequired = f(R(d)), with higher risk requiring stronger assurance, and argues formal-verification effort should itself be risk-weighted (strong guarantees for authorization/security/financial transitions/election integrity/production changes, not every UI label) -- 'pragmatic formal engineering'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Correctness as a multi-dimensional property: safety, liveness, fairness, deadlock, consistency (strong vs eventual)
b_rows_sample.statement: Writes a safety property as not-BadState for all reachable states and a liveness property as Request ⇒ Eventually(Response) under stated assumptions; adds fairness (ValidRequest ⇒ EventuallyProcessed given available resources) and notes deadlock as a case where Safety=True but Liveness=False (Decision_A waits for Decision_B which waits for A). Defines Correctness = {Safety, Liveness, Consistency, Traceability, EpistemicIntegrity, GovernanceCompliance}, not merely 'NoBug'. For consistency, distinguishes StrongConsistency from EventualConsistency (example: an audit record needs Strong, a search index may tolerate Eventual), so each invariant should carry an explicit ConsistencyRequirement (e.g. I_audit=Strong, I_search=Eventual); Conflict(C1,C2) between contradictory same-object claims must become explicit knowledge rather than silently resolved.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Invariant registry artifact and verification-method taxonomy with sound abstraction
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines an InvariantRegistry artifact where each invariant carries ID, owner bounded context, formal statement, criticality, enforcement point, verification method, failure policy, evidence, version, and status (worked example: INV-GOV-001, 'Production execution requires valid authorization', owned by Governance Context, Critical, enforced at the Decision Gate, verified by formal rule + integration test, failure=Block execution, v1.0); every invariant needs exactly one authoritative owner, preventing MultipleContexts -> ConflictingTruth. Lists verification methods (FormalProof, ModelChecking, PropertyBasedTest, IntegrationTest, RuntimeAssertion, HumanReview) with differing assurance levels, and defense-in-depth enforcement across Domain -> Application -> Infrastructure -> Runtime layers that must not create contradictory semantics. For property-based testing/model checking, notes state-space explosion (|Reach| can grow exponentially) requiring abstraction: alpha: ConcreteState -> AbstractState, with a sound abstraction requiring Violation_Concrete ⇒ Violation_Abstract for the property verified ('a key formal-methods principle') -- concluding KnowledgeOS does not need a theorem prover everywhere, but can combine FormalMethods + DeterministicRules + PropertyTests + StatisticalValidation + RuntimeChecks + Governance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Layered correctness and the first candidate KOSCorrect predicate
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Correctness = C_formal ∩ C_deterministic ∩ C_empirical ∩ C_epistemic ∩ C_governance -- 'a system can be mathematically correct but operationally invalid if governance is wrong'. Formulates the first candidate correctness contract: KOSCorrect iff I_global ∧ Contracts ∧ Safety ∧ Liveness ∧ Traceability ∧ EpistemicIntegrity, explicitly caveated as 'not yet a machine-checkable theorem... our architectural correctness specification'; the document explicitly warns against claiming KnowledgeOS 'has now been mathematically proven correct' -- the correct statement is that a candidate formal specification now exists against which correctness can be demonstrated.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Twelve falsification experiments for Step 48 global-invariant/correctness model (all PASS)
b_rows_sample.statement: Runs twelve falsification tests, all PASS: (1) a component is locally correct but its interface translation violates semantics => global invariant failure detected; (2) all safety properties hold but a workflow deadlocks => safety passes, liveness fails; (3) evidence is modified without a new version => evidence-integrity violation; (4) a decision uses a model created after the decision date => temporal/historical-integrity violation; (5) an AI proposal bypasses authorization => AI-boundary and authorization invariants fail; (6) a causal claim has no documented assumptions => causal-integrity violation; (7) a trusted claim becomes invalid but remains operational without review => revision/invalidation-invariant violation; (8) a safety-critical unknown is treated as true => unknown-state/safety-invariant violation; (9) a claim valid in one bounded context is applied to another without semantic mapping => scope/semantic-integrity violation; (10) two distributed replicas temporarily disagree where eventual consistency is permitted => no violation if the declared consistency contract allows it; (11) two replicas disagree on a strong-consistency invariant => critical consistency violation; (12) a model is stable and highly confident but external validation shows systematic error => epistemic correctness fails despite model stability.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Three-level distinction: MathematicalConsistency / ReferenceMachineConsistency / ProductionSystemCorrectness; PASS != production-proven
b_rows_sample.statement: Issues a scientific correction on the word PASS: these are formal reference-machine experiments, not evidence a production implementation has passed. Establishes 'the specified machine has a coherent execution path under the tested scenarios' but explicitly not ProductionImplementationCorrect. Introduces three levels: Level 1 MathematicalConsistency (tested in Steps 49-50); Level 2 ReferenceMachineConsistency (specified and exercised in Steps 51/56); Level 3 ProductionSystemCorrectness (not yet demonstrated) -- 'this distinction is extremely important'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Precise falsification criterion for safety □I(X_t) and liveness ◇Goal; safety evidence currently stronger than liveness evidence
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives a precise falsification criterion: finding X_t with I(X_t)=True where a valid transition produces I(X_{t+1})=False would be a genuine architectural failure; finding a ValidDomainState with no valid transition despite the domain requiring progress would expose a liveness defect. Formalizes Safety as Box I(X_t) (something bad never happens) and Liveness as Diamond Goal (something good eventually happens), and states KnowledgeOS currently has substantially stronger evidence for safety than for liveness -- 'an important scientific qualification'. Illustrates the liveness gap: a system can preserve every invariant and still get stuck in Decision -> Waiting -> Waiting -> Waiting with no invariant violated, yet the workflow has failed.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.13 — Verification versus validation ... Verification: did we build the system according to its formal specification? Validation: does the specification/model actually represent the real system adequately? Both are necessary.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Verification (built according to formal spec) from Validation (spec adequately represents reality); both are necessary.

b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8: an internally consistent model of the wrong business process shows Verification=True but Validation=False; result PASS.
