a_rows_sample.anchor: They may support the same proposition p=HasVersion(S,v1) while remaining distinct evidence objects. Therefore we need at least three relations: Identity, Equality, Support. These must not be conflated.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes via a two-observation example (o1 by System A at t1, o2 by System B at t2, both supporting the same proposition p) that Identity, Equality, and Support must be three distinct, non-conflatable relations: distinct observations can support the same proposition without being identical or equal to each other.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS may require domain identity in addition to mathematical equality ... a possible distinction is: StructuralEqual(x,y) versus SameIdentity(x,y). This is not yet an accepted KnowledgeOS definition. It is a required question.
a_rows_sample.statement: Poses object-level StructuralEqual(x,y) versus SameIdentity(x,y) as a required, not-yet-answered distinction: two records may be structurally identical while referring to different historical occurrences, so domain identity may be needed beyond ordinary mathematical equality.

a_rows_sample.anchor: There are at least four possibilities. A. Syntactic equality ... B. Semantic equality ... C. Observational equality ... D. Provenance-sensitive equality ... These are not interchangeable.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines four non-interchangeable candidate Knowledge-State equality relations: syntactic (byte/structural identity), semantic (same knowledge semantics), observational (same result under every permitted observation), and provenance-sensitive (content and relevant provenance equivalent).

a_rows_sample.anchor: K1={p,e1} and K2={p,e2} where e1!=e2 but Supports(e1,p) and Supports(e2,p). Should K1=K2? There is no obvious answer. ... This proves that equality cannot be defined until we know what constitutes semantically essential information. Equality depends on the ontology and semantics.
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives a worked counterexample (two states differing only in which distinct evidence item supports the same proposition) showing equality is undecidable until it is settled whether provenance is semantically constitutive of knowledge identity or merely metadata -- concluding equality is ontology/semantics-dependent, not free-standing.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The mandate explicitly tells us not to assume this dependency ordering [G1->G2->G3]. ... the dependency graph is more accurately: Ontology -> State Representation -> Semantic Identity -> Equality ... So G1->G3 is plausible, but G1->G2->G3 is not established.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects a previously assumed linear dependency ordering (G1: what is a KnowledgeState -> G2: what is epistemic status -> G3: what is equality) into a revised chain Ontology -> State Representation -> Semantic Identity -> Equality, with epistemic status interacting with both representation and equality rather than sitting strictly between state-definition and equality; the direct G1->G2->G3 chain is explicitly downgraded to not established.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The propositions may refer to different times ... Then there is no contradiction. This demonstrates that contradiction cannot be determined from proposition content alone. ... A better candidate is: Contradicts(p1,p2,c) ... contradiction is likely a derived semantic relation, not a primitive field o
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows via a temporal-interval example (HasVersion(S,v1) valid on [t1,t2), HasVersion(S,v2) valid on [t2,t3)) that two propositions with conflicting content are not automatically contradictory, since contradiction depends on context c as well as content; concludes contradiction is a derived semantic relation Contradicts(p1,p2,c), not a primitive Knowledge-State field.

a_rows_sample.anchor: with both assert validity over exactly the same interval ... If the domain invariant is: forall t: #Version(S,t)<=1, then Contradicts(p1,p2)=true. ... Contradiction required: proposition semantics; temporal validity; domain constraints. Contradiction is not merely a property of two strings.
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives a strong-contradiction example: two version propositions over the identical time interval, evaluated against an explicit domain invariant (a service has at most one version at any time) actually do produce Contradicts=true, demonstrating contradiction requires jointly proposition semantics, temporal validity, and domain constraints -- it is a relation evaluated under a semantic regime, not a syntactic property.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A logical regime could define Contradiction_L. A temporal regime could define Contradiction_T. A probabilistic regime might instead calculate P(p1|E) and P(p2|E). These need not produce the same classification. Contradiction may be regime-relative.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes that contradiction may be regime-relative: a logical regime, a temporal regime, and a probabilistic regime applied to the same pair of propositions need not agree on whether a contradiction exists -- a stronger claim than merely 'KnowledgeOS supports contradictions', and supportive of a multi-regime architecture operating over a common substrate.

a_rows_sample.anchor: P(p)=0.7 ... It could represent: probability of truth; confidence in an observation; reliability of a source; posterior probability; frequency in a population; degree of belief; probability of an answer. These are mathematically different quantities. 0.7 alone has no epistemic semantics.
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues a bare numeric uncertainty value (e.g. P(p)=0.7) has no epistemic semantics on its own, since it could denote any of at least 7 mathematically distinct quantities (probability of truth, observation confidence, source reliability, posterior probability, population frequency, degree of belief, or probability of an answer) -- reinforcing an earlier corpus warning against identifying measurement/probability with knowledge itself.

a_rows_sample.anchor: P_M(p|E) has a meaningful interpretation relative to M. This is fundamentally different from asserting p=0.7. ... K --probabilistic regime--> D ... A probability distribution may be a regime-specific representation over a knowledge-state space [not] KnowledgeOS = Probability Distribution. The latter
a_rows_sample.statement: Relocates probability from being a property directly assigned to a proposition (p=0.7) to a projection K --regime--> D produced by an explicit probabilistic model M (P_M(p|E)); explicitly rejects the earlier corpus formulation 'KnowledgeOS = Application + Distribution + Measure' as a category error, preserving instead the weaker claim that a probability distribution may be one regime-specific representation over the knowledge-state space.

a_rows_sample.anchor: not every numerical assignment licenses arithmetic operations ... c(p)+c(q) is not automatically meaningful. Nor is 2c(p). Numeric representation != quantitative measurement.
a_rows_sample.statement: Invokes a Roberts-style measurement-theory constraint: a numerical assignment is meaningful only when its empirical relational structure and representation theorem justify it, so arithmetic operations on a stored confidence/uncertainty number (e.g. c(p)+c(q), 2*c(p)) are not automatically meaningful -- numeric representation is not the same as quantitative measurement, a constraint relevant to any future statistical regime.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge Substrate plus Semantic Relations plus Epistemic Qualifications plus Regime Specific Projections rather than one homogeneous mathematical object containing every possible quantity. ... Projection_R: K x R -> Y_R where K = knowledge substrate; R = regime; Y_R = regime-specific representatio
a_rows_sample.statement: Converges on a 4-part architectural decomposition (Knowledge Substrate, Semantic Relations, Epistemic Qualifications, Regime-Specific Projections) rather than one homogeneous state object, formalized as a candidate interface Projection_R: K x R -> Y_R (K=substrate, R=regime, Y_R=regime output), instantiated for logical (LogicalModel), probabilistic (Distribution), measurement (MeasurementSpace) and governance (Decision/ComplianceAssessment) regimes -- explicitly not yet the final architecture but a testable interface.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A regime may transform or interpret a knowledge substrate, but it must not silently change the historical identity of the underlying knowledge objects. ... the projection should preserve the identity mapping id_K: K -> K. A regime-specific representation must not silently turn e1 into e2.
a_rows_sample.statement: States a candidate cross-regime invariant: any regime projection Pi_R(K)=Y_R must preserve the identity mapping id_K:K->K on the underlying knowledge objects -- a regime interpretation must never silently substitute one evidence/knowledge object's identity for another's, which is particularly important for provenance.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS must distinguish the epistemic substrate from the mathematical regimes used to interpret it. ... Probability != Knowledge. Measurement != Knowledge. Logical inference != Knowledge. but all may operate on knowledge under properly defined regimes.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the step's central principle: KnowledgeOS must distinguish the epistemic substrate from the mathematical regimes (logical, probabilistic, measurement) used to interpret it -- Probability != Knowledge, Measurement != Knowledge, Logical inference != Knowledge, though all may legitimately operate on knowledge as regimes; noted as independently arrived at, matching an existing corpus warning against equating the epistemic core with measure theory.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Is the candidate Knowledge State actually a state, or is it fundamentally a history/process? ... We therefore need to test K_t versus H_t=(K_0,T_1,T_2,...,T_t) and determine whether K_t is sufficient to reconstruct everything that KnowledgeOS claims to preserve. ... the true formal object may be clo
a_rows_sample.statement: Sets up the next test (named Step 247, State vs. History Sufficiency Test): whether the candidate Knowledge State K_t is sufficient by itself, or whether the true formal object must be a state-history pair (K_t, H_t) with H_t=(K0,T1,...,Tt), given the corpus's repeated emphasis on provenance/transformation/history as central rather than a single lineage component.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Can two knowledge states be identical while having different histories? If yes, then History(K) != K may be fundamental. Construct an example K1 and K2 with identical current semantic content but different histories. Then test K1=K2 under: structural, semantic, provenance-sensitive, historical ident
a_rows_sample.statement: Mandates testing whether lambda (lineage) belongs inside K, outside K, or as a derived function History:K->Histories, via a required counterexample construction: two states with identical current semantic content but different histories, tested against 4 equality notions (structural, semantic, provenance-sensitive, historical identity) to determine whether History(K) != K is fundamental.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K1 and K2 with identical content, status, temporality and policy -- differing only in history ... structural: False, semantic: True, provenance-sensitive: False, historical identity: False. ... History(K) != K is fundamental. lambda belongs OUTSIDE K, as History: K -> Histories.
a_rows_sample.statement: Constructs two states K1/K2 identical in content/status/temporality/policy but differing in history, computing all four equality relations from the earlier stress test (structural=False, semantic=True, provenance-sensitive=False, historical identity=False), demonstrating semantic equality can be TRUE while historical identity is FALSE -- proving a single tuple containing lambda cannot express both relations at once, and that including lambda in K makes structural equality history-sensitive, breaking deduplication and merge. Verdict: History(K)!=K is fundamental; lambda belongs outside K as History:K->Histories, mathematically verified, and aligned with the real implementation (a separate lineage graph, no KnowledgeState).

a_rows_sample.anchor: The equality blocker DISSOLVES once the assertion layer is restored. It was unsolvable at the level of K alone because identity lives one level down. [equality table: proposition identity, assertion identity, assertion structural/semantic equality, knowledge-state equality, historical identity -- al
a_rows_sample.statement: Resolves the equality blocker (open since S1601/S1603) by showing all 6 candidate equality relations (proposition identity, assertion identity via id, assertion structural equality, assertion semantic equality ignoring evidence ids, pointwise knowledge-state equality, and historical identity as a distinct 6th relation via History(K1)=History(K2)) become computable once identity and equality are defined at the assertion level rather than forced onto K directly.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I proposed a four-state set (Unknown/Supported/Refuted/Conflicted). That is one too many. group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 's1604-theory-discovery-phase-mandate' POSSIBLY relates to 's1602-formal-system-reconstruction-mandate' (batch B0039). Note: The mandate that ends sequential step-auditing in favor of gap-driven theory reconstruction; preserves S1603's FORMALLY INCOMPLETE verdict as a starting candidate; introduces the AUTHOR INPUT REQUIRED marker and a formal author-consultation protocol (STOP + 7-field brief) for normative-only decisions, a 3-way historical/mathematical/engineering question separation, a 5-representation test for K, a 9-way decomposition of 'validity', and a load-bearing-blocker (not percentage) completeness framing.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Model A -- State-sufficient: K_t is sufficient; H_t is reconstructable or non-essential. Model B -- History-essential: the actual KnowledgeOS object is K_t=(K_t,H_t) where H_t=(K_0,T_1,...,T_t). The question is therefore whether two histories can produce the same apparent state while remaining seman
a_rows_sample.statement: Poses two explicit competing models for the fundamental KnowledgeOS object: Model A (state-sufficient, K_t alone suffices, history is external/reconstructable provenance) versus Model B (history-essential, the real object is a pair (K_t,H_t)) -- to be decided by whether two histories producing the same apparent state can remain semantically different.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose the current content is identical: Content(K1)=Content(K'1). ... e_A != e_B. And therefore H_A != H_B. ... If provenance is semantically relevant: K1 != K'1. If provenance is merely explanatory metadata: K1 = K'1. We cannot choose between them by mathematical elegance. ... History essentialit
a_rows_sample.statement: Constructs a counterexample (two histories with different supporting evidence e_A!=e_B but identical resulting content) leaving whether the two resulting states should be considered equal genuinely unresolved: it depends on whether provenance is semantically constitutive (states differ) or merely explanatory metadata (states are equal) -- explicitly stating this cannot be decided by mathematical elegance alone and remains open.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Can two states with identical current representation produce different valid future behavior? ... If T(K_A)=K'_A and T(K_B)=K'_B with K'_A not equiv K'_B, then history affects future semantics. In that case, the compressed state K is not sufficient. This gives us a rigorous state sufficiency criteri
a_rows_sample.statement: Reframes the provenance-metadata-vs-constitutive question into a testable future-behavior criterion avoiding philosophical argument: if two states with identical current representation but different history produce different results under the same transformation, then the state representation is insufficient -- directly the criterion S1608 (Step 248) then executes.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A state representation K_t is sufficient if future evolution depends only on K_t and the future inputs: P(K_{t+1}|K_t,H_t,I_{t+1}) = P(K_{t+1}|K_t,I_{t+1}). ... this does not mean KnowledgeOS is a Markov process. It gives us a test for whether the proposed state representation has the Markov-style s
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes state sufficiency via an explicit analogy to the Markov property (K_t is sufficient iff conditioning on the full history H_t adds no information about K_{t+1} beyond K_t and the input), carefully distinguishing this from a claim that KnowledgeOS literally is a Markov process -- it is offered only as a formal sufficiency test, borrowed from stochastic-process theory.

a_rows_sample.anchor: If H_t = f(lambda_t), then history may not need to be a separate primitive. Instead: Lineage could be a sufficient compressed representation of history. ... (K_t,H_t) is unnecessary if K_t=(Content_t,lambda_t,...) already contains all semantically relevant historical information.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes the lineage-as-sufficient-compression hypothesis: if the full history H_t can be reconstructed from the lineage component lambda_t alone (H_t=f(lambda_t)), then the state-history pair (K_t,H_t) collapses back to a single sufficient state K_t=(Content_t,lambda_t,...), making lineage an important candidate compression of history rather than a separate primitive.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose they produce identical lineage edges. Yet the transformations had different policies pi_A != pi_B. If policy is semantically relevant, then lambda_A=lambda_B does not imply H_A = H_B. ... Potentially lambda=(source,transformation,actor,time,policy,evidence). But this is again a candidate str
a_rows_sample.statement: Falsifies plain parent-child lineage as a sufficient history compression: two histories can produce identical lineage edges while having been governed by different policies, so if policy is semantically relevant then lineage-equality does not imply history-equivalence -- proposing a richer candidate lambda=(source,transformation,actor,time,policy,evidence), still only a candidate structure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: State_t = fold(T_1,...,T_t,K_0). This suggests H_t can generate K_t. But H_t -> K_t does not imply K_t -> H_t. The fold can be many-to-one. ... Two different histories can converge on the same state. Therefore state compression generally loses historical information.
a_rows_sample.statement: Uses an event-sourcing fold analogy (State_t=fold(T1,...,Tt,K0)) to show history-generates-state does not imply state-determines-history: the fold is generically many-to-one (distinct transformation sequences can converge on the same state), so state compression generically loses historical information -- the analogy is explicitly flagged as useful but not proof.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Which equivalence relation on histories defines semantic state equality? ... H_1 ~_H H_2 iff they are semantically indistinguishable for all permitted KnowledgeOS operations. a_rows_sample.statement: Reframes the compression problem sharply as: which equivalence relation ~_H on the space of histories (semantic indistinguishability under all permitted operations) actually defines Knowledge-State equality; proposes the candidate mathematical definition Knowledge State = [H]_{~_H}, an equivalence class of histories, as an alternative to 'Knowledge State = the current graph' -- explicitly a candidate formulation pending corpus validation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: That requires: H_1 ~_H H_2 => T(H_1) ~_H T(H_2). This is a congruence condition. If it holds, the transformation descends from histories to states. ... State abstraction is valid only if it is transformation-compatible.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The question is now: lambda sufficient to make the state abstraction transformation-compatible? We do not know yet. ... a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a 3-level candidate architecture H --F--> K --Projection_R--> Y_R (history, then abstracted state, then a regime-specific representation such as logic, probability, measurement, or governance), extending the Step-246 (S1601) Projection_R interface by placing it explicitly downstream of the history-to-state abstraction F.

a_rows_sample.anchor: STATE-ONLY MODEL: NOT YET PROVEN. HISTORY-ESSENTIAL MODEL: NOT YET PROVEN. STATE-AS-HISTORY-EQUIVALENCE-CLASS: STRONG CANDIDATE. LINEAGE-AS-SUFFICIENT-COMPRESSION: KEY HYPOTHESIS TO TEST. ... the problem has been reduced to a precise mathematical criterion.
a_rows_sample.statement: Records the Step-247 verdict: neither the state-only model nor the history-essential model is proven; the state-as-history-equivalence-class formulation is rated a strong mathematical candidate; lineage-as-sufficient-compression is named the key hypothesis to test next -- reframing the vague 'is KnowledgeOS a state or a history' question into the precise, testable criterion of whether the state abstraction defines a congruence over transformations.

a_rows_sample.anchor: H1 ~_H H2 iff all permitted future operation sequences produce equivalent states. a_rows_sample.statement: Strengthens history equivalence beyond the naive current-state-collapse definition into full behavioral equivalence (agreement of outcomes under every admissible future operation sequence, not just the current state), reaffirming Step 247's (S1609) candidate quotient definition K=[H]_{~_H} as a powerful but still unproven formulation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K* = H / equiv_T where [H] = {H' in H | H' equiv_T H}. The candidate state is therefore an equivalence class of histories. A Knowledge State need not be the history itself; it can be the semantic information that distinguishes one behavioral class of histories from another.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We must not define K* as: the tuple with the fewest fields. That would be an engineering compression criterion, not a semantic minimality criterion. ... Semantic minimality != syntactic compactness.

b_rows_sample.statement: Proves the 3 standard equivalence-relation properties for the candidate observational equivalence: reflexivity only provisionally (fails to be automatic if observations are stochastic/nondeterministic/environment-dependent), symmetry and transitivity both derived under ordinary equality -- all three still depend on the eventual full closure and definition of the permitted-observation set O.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K* = H / equiv_T where [H] = {H' in H | H' equiv_T H}. The candidate state is therefore an equivalence class of histories. A Knowledge State need not be the history itself; it can be the semantic information that distinguishes one behavioral class of histories from another.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the candidate quotient construction K*=H/equiv_T (equivalence classes of histories under the congruence-respecting relation) as conceptually powerful precisely because a Knowledge State need not literally be the history, only the semantic information distinguishing behavioral classes -- the final, most rigorous form of Step 247's (S1609) equivalence-class hypothesis.

b_rows_sample.anchor: If no such representation is available under the required constraints, then the mathematical theory may exist but fail computationally. This is not a contradiction. It would be: Mathematically valid, computationally unusable.
b_rows_sample.statement: Names the specific, non-contradictory failure mode of a mathematically valid but computationally unusable theory: a quotient can exist abstractly with no effective encode/decode mapping to a finite representation available under KnowledgeOS's actual constraints.

Composability is not automatic from quotient existence. ... If Merge(H1,H2) not-equiv Merge(H1',H2'), then Merge does not descend to the
b_rows_sample.statement: Proves Composability of Merge over the quotient is a distinct congruence requirement (representative-independence: equivalent inputs must produce equivalent Merge outputs), not automatic from mere quotient existence; if it fails, Merge simply does not descend to a well-defined K* x K* -> K* operation, requiring one of 5 named remedies (a richer K, additional external context, a restricted Merge domain, a partial operation, or a different semantic interpretation).

a_rows_sample.statement: Finds 'Assurance' irreparably overloaded across 31 definitional statements collapsing into 6 mutually incompatible types (composed local contracts, a function of irreversibility/impact/criticality, a 'Strong BC Candidate' label, BackwardTraceability, a self-referential DeterministicAssurance, and a plain boolean); Step 230's self-referential definition directly contradicts the corpus's own imported Williamson result that assurance cannot recursively certify itself; and by the corpus's own most-repeated epistemological claim (assurance is strong only where executable, weak where prose), the corpus's own assurance concept is weak -- named completion blocker CB-1, a hard blocker on formal closure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: (K, Merge, empty) is a commutative idempotent monoid -- a JOIN-SEMILATTICE. Executed. ... Contradict is symmetric, irreflexive, and NOT transitive -- a tolerance relation, never an equivalence. Any construction treating contradiction as an equivalence class is wrong. ... a_rows_sample.statement: Extends S1612's proven results with 5 further executed algebraic facts: (K,Merge,empty-set) forms a commutative idempotent monoid, i.e. a join-semilattice; Contradict is symmetric and irreflexive but NOT transitive, making it a tolerance relation rather than an equivalence (any equivalence-class-based construction on contradiction is wrong); Remove has no total inverse (cascading removal loses relations R, non-cascading breaks Valid); Split is lossy on R; and Merge preserves structural validity but not consistency, demonstrated by an executed counterexample where two individually consistent states merge into a contradictory one.

a_rows_sample.statement: Reports 5 executed empirical probes against real systems this session: knowledge-lint.php passes on all 37 governed documents (exit 0); knowledge-graph.php run twice produces byte-identical 39-node/70-edge output (deterministic); php artisan test filters confirm 47/125 (Lineage) and 10/34 (KnowledgeOs) assertions passing, corroborating the '47 tests passing' figure independently found elsewhere in this batch (S1595, S1600); and a 14-probe reference model run passes 13/14, with the one failure diagnosed as genuine theory content (Section 8).

a_rows_sample.statement: Finds 4 independent corroborations from unrelated production bounded contexts (convergent evolution, not KnowledgeOS-derived): ReplayAssertion uses a content hash (including time) as identity, captures policy externally, has no status field, and is documented immutable -- matching the S1595 identity-repair direction; EvidenceSet holds evidence strictly by reference, never by value (ADR-T16), exactly matching the corpus derivation's rejection of embedding evidence objects; EventProvenance uses (correlationId,causationId), explicitly scoped to Integration Events only; and authorities.yaml documents governance status as independent of lifecycle status, meaning Sigma-perp-Gamma orthogonality (S1606) is enforced in running production configuration by a linter, not merely a theoretical derivation.

a_rows_sample.statement: Resolves the open Provenance/Lineage distinction (S1600, S1616) into a definitive three-way finding: Pi (an assertion's own origin, per Q7), History(T) (the state's transformation record, as implemented in GovernanceLineageGraph), and EventProvenance (a message causal chain, correlationId/causationId, used only for Integration Events in production) are three genuinely distinct objects sharing one overloaded word -- the verification programme itself had conflated the first two prior to this phase, and the third (EventProvenance) had been entirely invisible to the corpus.

a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces a 3-way taxonomy of history dependence: Type I intrinsic-state dependence (part of what the knowledge state means, e.g. epistemic standing, belongs inside K); Type II transformation-context dependence (affects transformation evaluation without being knowledge content, e.g. Policy, supplied as an external T parameter); Type III audit/history dependence (needed for reconstruction/explanation/accountability without necessarily altering knowledge identity, e.g. Provenance) -- pinpointing Provenance's placement as exactly the Type-III unresolved case.

a_rows_sample.statement: Applies Step 255's finding directly: no operation should be forced into the shape T:K->K, since operations may legitimately depend on external typed context (policy, authority, time, evidence) rather than K alone.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Add requires a definition of identity/equality. This directly links Step 256 back to the unresolved Equality_K. ... set-like semantics Add(K,x)=K union {x} [versus] identity-aware semantics [which] may reject an object whose identity already exists.
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows Add cannot be formally defined until equality/identity is resolved, since two radically different semantics remain open: plain set-union (duplicates silently absorbed) versus identity-aware rejection of objects whose identity already exists.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Does removal mean x not-in K' or x in K' with status Withdrawn? These are radically different semantics. ... Remove != Withdraw unless the vocabulary explicitly decides otherwise. ... Reject(x) != Remove(x). This is an important Ubiquitous Language distinction.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes true deletion from lifecycle-status change as radically different operation semantics, concluding Remove != Withdraw and Reject != Remove unless the theory explicitly decides to identify them -- since a status-changed object remains represented in K while a deleted one does not.

a_rows_sample.anchor: revision requires identity preservation: id(x')=id(x)? If yes, Revision(x,x') is a state transition on one entity. If no, Revision is actually Remove(x)+Add(x'). ... What makes two knowledge objects 'the same object' across revision? ... This is another reason why equality and identity cannot be pos
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows Revise cannot be formally defined until cross-time object identity is resolved: if id(x')=id(x), Revise is a genuine state transition on one entity; if not, Revise reduces to Remove+Add of two different entities -- the same identity/equality dependency recurring across multiple operations.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Provenance(x3) = {Provenance(x1), Provenance(x2)}. If so, Merge is inherently provenance-preserving. This means that the operation registry itself can reveal whether provenance is operationally essential. ... Split requires a preservation invariant.
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows Merge is diagnostically important for the provenance question: if the merged object's provenance is the union of its sources' provenances, Merge is inherently provenance-preserving, meaning the operation registry itself (not abstract argument) can reveal whether provenance is operationally essential; separately notes Split requires an explicit semantic-preservation invariant across its decomposition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Every semantically relevant external variable must be explicit. ... T: K x Policy x Time -> K'. This is preferable to hiding Policy or Time inside an implicit global context. ... Deterministic Transformation != Immutable Knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: States a determinism-discipline principle: any externally-varying quantity a transformation depends on (e.g. current time, applicable policy) must be an explicit function argument, never an implicit global, or the transformation appears nondeterministic to the mathematical model; separately clarifies determinism (same inputs, same result) is orthogonal to immutability of the overall knowledge base.

a_rows_sample.anchor: R(T_i) = (Name, Domain, Codomain, Preconditions, Postconditions, Invariants, Parameters, Dependencies, Determinism, ProvenanceDependency, HistoryDependency, PolicyDependency, IdentityDependency) becomes the working registry schema.

a_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms the corpus's established finding that the governed transformation subset is not closed under composition, applying it to the operation-registry construction: composition T_j o T_i is only meaningful when Codomain(T_i) intersects Domain(T_j), and closure must never be assumed.

a_rows_sample.anchor: T_Add: K x X -> K, T_Merge: K x X x X -> K, Validate: K x E -> Result, Approve: Candidate x Authority -> ApprovedCandidate. Therefore KnowledgeOS may be better modeled as a typed transition system than as a single algebra.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Validate not-equiv Transform. This prevents a common category error in the kernel. ... Command is not Transformation ... Command -> Decision -> Transformation -> NewState ... Event != T. The corpus already distinguishes Command -> Transformation -> Event.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms three category-error-preventing non-collapses for the operation vocabulary: Validate != Transform (validation may determine valid/invalid without changing K); Command != Transformation (command is intent/request, not the state change itself); Event != Transformation (an event records an occurrence, distinct from the state-evolution-defining function).

a_rows_sample.statement: Converts the recurring vague 'does provenance belong in K' question into a precise operational test using explicit per-operation dependency flags (ProvDep, HistDep, PolicyDep in {0,1,?}): if any operation has ProvDep=1, provenance-sensitive information must be accessible to it, and only then does the placement question (K-resident, T-parameter, or external context) arise -- directly implementing S1621's Type-I/II/III taxonomy as a concrete research tool.

a_rows_sample.statement: Refines the kernel-minimization target by splitting an operation's total required information into StateReq(T) (must be resident in K) and ContextReq(T) (may be supplied externally, does not constrain K), restating the optimization target K*=argmin Complexity(K) subject to semantic sufficiency with this refined split.

a_rows_sample.statement: Consolidates the step's established-versus-not-established results: established that T must be typed before K can be minimized, operations may be partial, need not share one signature, and 4 key terms must not be conflated, with dependency-testing mandatory per operation; explicitly not established that the 9 candidate operations or any particular signature is final.

Step 257 -- Formalize the Four Discriminating Operations ... Then we can run the first real congruence experiment ... That
a_rows_sample.statement: Names Supersede, Merge, Revise and Transform as the 4 highest-value operations for distinguishing competing state/history models, and sets Step 257 as their complete formalization (across domain/codomain/preconditions/postconditions/identity/provenance/history/policy/determinism/composability) in order to run the first real congruence experiment -- explicitly judged stronger evidence than proposing yet another candidate kernel tuple.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 12 operations fully specified [create, assert, retract, relate, merge, supersede, refine, resolve, remove, replay, validate, assess] each with Input/Preconditions/Output/Postconditions/Det/Auth/Gov/Hist/Computable/Failure modes. All 12 rated Computable=YES.
a_rows_sample.statement: Fully specifies concrete 11-field signatures for 12 named operations (create, assert, retract, relate, merge, supersede, refine, resolve, remove, replay, validate, assess), each rated computable=YES, directly executing the operation-registry schema Step 256 (S1623) had proposed abstractly -- e.g. retract has failure mode LOSSY-NO-INVERSE (executed), relate can fail via a cycle, merge may introduce contradiction (executed), replay is order-dependent (executed).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Model R1 -- Identity-preserving revision: id(x_old)=id(x_new). Model R2 -- Replacement revision: id(x_old)!=id(x_new), effectively Remove(x_old)+Add(x_new). These models have different implications for lineage. Revision semantics require an explicit identity rule.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Revision history is necessary only if future semantics observe it. This is the congruence principle from Step 255. ... Prov(x1)=Prov(x0) union {e} or perhaps Prov(x1)={e}. These are not equivalent. Prov(Revise) remains unresolved.
b_rows_sample.statement: Applies Step 255's congruence principle to Revise specifically (revision history matters only if a mandatory future operation observes it), and separately leaves the provenance-composition rule for Revise unresolved (does the revised object's provenance union with, or replace, its predecessor's).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Supersede => Identity, but does not establish Identity subseteq K until we know whether identity is represented in the state or externally resolvable. ... Temporal order != Supersession relation. ... A provenance-preserving model may require Prov(x2) superset-or-equal Prov(x1). But perhaps the super
b_rows_sample.statement: Establishes 3 findings for Supersede: it requires stable identity for both operands (Supersede implies Identity, without settling whether identity lives in K); temporal event-ordering (t1<t2) must not be conflated with semantic supersession precedence (x2 succ x1) -- they are logically independent; and provenance propagation under supersession cannot be assumed equal between old and new, requiring an explicit rule.

b_rows_sample.anchor: H1: x0->x1 with x1 succ x0. H2: x1. If SupersessionHistory(x1) is semantically observable, then H1 and H2 cannot be collapsed. If no mandatory operation observes supersession history, then the histories may be equivalent. Therefore this is a conditional counterexample.
b_rows_sample.statement: Constructs a conditional (not established) counterexample for Supersede: whether two histories differing only in supersession lineage but sharing the same current object must be distinguished depends entirely on whether any mandatory operation actually observes supersession history.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Three possible Merge identity semantics: New identity id(x3)!=id(x1),id(x2); One-source identity retained id(x3)=id(x1); Composite identity id(x3)=f(id(x1),id(x2)). The corpus does not establish which model is correct. Merge cannot be fully typed until identity semantics are fixed.
b_rows_sample.statement: Poses 3 mutually exclusive identity semantics for the result of Merge (entirely new identity, one source's identity retained, or a composite function of both sources' identities), none established by the corpus, concluding Merge cannot be fully typed until this is resolved.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Prov(x3) superset-or-equal Prov(x1) union Prov(x2). If that invariant is mandatory, then Merge is provenance-sensitive. ... This experiment therefore directly tests the architectural placement of provenance. ... Merge requires a semantic preservation invariant [Meaning(x3) must relate appropriately
b_rows_sample.statement: Identifies Merge as the strongest available operational test for provenance placement: if a mandatory provenance-union invariant holds, Merge is provenance-sensitive and this experiment directly tests where provenance architecturally belongs; separately notes Merge requires an unspecified, domain-specific semantic-preservation invariant relating the merged meaning to its sources' meanings.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The four operations do not require identical semantic inputs. Therefore a single universal signature T:KxP->K is likely too coarse. Instead T = {T1,...,Tn} should be treated as a typed family. ... Operation dependency != State membership. Transform(K,Policy) does not imply Policy subseteq K. Similar
b_rows_sample.statement: Confirms via the 4-operation dependency comparison that a single universal transformation signature is too coarse (the operations need different inputs), reinforcing the typed-family conclusion, and restates the operation-dependency != state-membership principle with concrete Transform/Policy and Merge/Evidence examples.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The strongest dependencies are currently: Supersede => Identity, Revise => Identity, Merge => Identity, and potentially Merge => Provenance. ... This means identity may be a more fundamental candidate for K than some of the earlier kernel components. But that remains a candidate, not a conclusion.
b_rows_sample.statement: Aggregates the per-operation dependency findings, showing Identity is required by 3 of the 4 discriminating operations (Supersede, Revise, Merge) and Provenance potentially by a 4th aspect (Merge), tentatively elevating Identity to a more fundamental kernel candidate than some earlier components -- explicitly flagged as a candidate, not a proven conclusion.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We previously treated Equality_K as foundational. But operationally, Identity must first be distinguished from Equality. Two states can be equal while containing different historical identities, depending on the chosen equivalence. Identity != Equality. The theory needs both concepts, even if they e
b_rows_sample.statement: States the step's fourth major finding, reordering the theory's foundational priorities: Identity must be distinguished from Equality operationally, contrary to earlier treatment of Equality_K as the sole foundational relation -- two states can be equal under a chosen equivalence while containing different historical identities, so both concepts are independently needed.

b_rows_sample.anchor: id(x1)=id(x2) does not necessarily imply x1=x2 as values. Likewise x1=x2 under extensional equality does not necessarily tell us whether they arose from the same lineage. This distinction will become critical in Step 258.
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives the formal separation between identity persistence (id(x1)=id(x2)) and value/extensional equality (x1=x2): neither implies the other, since identical identity does not guarantee identical current values, and extensional equality does not reveal shared lineage.

b_rows_sample.anchor: History dependence of implementation != History dependence of state semantics. ... The operation might internally inspect history while still producing the same semantically relevant state. ... Only the second disproves state sufficiency.
b_rows_sample.statement: Draws a critical architectural distinction between an operation's implementation inspecting history internally (That(H1)!=That(H2)) versus history actually affecting the resulting semantic state (F(That(H1))!=F(That(H2))) -- only the latter disproves state sufficiency; an operation may legitimately look at history while still producing an observably identical state.

b_rows_sample.anchor: the provenance base-case counterexample alone does not establish that provenance belongs in K. It establishes only that provenance cannot be reconstructed from transformation history alone. ... External provenance is information-theoretically irreducible from T-history, but it is not yet proven sema
b_rows_sample.statement: Sharpens the recurring provenance conclusion into its most defensible final form, explicitly proposed as a permanent theory distinction: external provenance is information-theoretically irreducible from transformation history (proven), but this does NOT prove provenance is semantically constitutive of the Knowledge State itself (not proven) -- it may remain purely audit/lineage information without being part of K's identity/equality.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Revise: identity + provenance semantics unresolved (yellow). Transform: exact context signature unresolved (yellow/green). Supersede: identity + temporal/provenance semantics unresolved (yellow). Merge: identity + preservation/provenance unresolved (yellow). These are now sufficiently structured to
b_rows_sample.statement: Reports the post-Step-257 formalization status of all 4 discriminating operations, each still carrying unresolved identity and/or provenance dependencies but now sufficiently structured to serve as concrete experimental test cases for the congruence criterion.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The next step should therefore isolate the issue that all four operations depend upon: Identity and Equality. ... Step 258 -- Identity, Equality and Knowledge-State Equivalence. When are two Knowledge Objects the same? and separately: When are two Knowledge States equivalent? These must not be confl
b_rows_sample.statement: Sets Step 258 to isolate Identity and Equality as the common dependency of all 4 discriminating operations, requiring 3 explicitly distinct relations (object equality =_X, Knowledge-State equivalence equiv_K, history equivalence cong_H, never conflated) and a congruence requirement (equiv_K preserved by every mandatory transformation) as the decisive criterion for whether a proposed equivalence is a legitimate semantic quotient.

b_rows_sample.anchor: =_I cannot by itself be the semantic equality relation [fails Revise, which requires semantic change while identity persists]. ... Content equality cannot replace identity [fails Merge/Supersede, which must distinguish independently-created identical-content objects].
b_rows_sample.statement: Proves both identity-only equality and content-only equality are individually insufficient as the semantic equality relation: identity-only equality cannot represent Revise (which needs semantic change while identity persists); content-only equality cannot represent Merge/Supersede (which must distinguish two independently-created objects with identical content).

b_rows_sample.anchor: For a composition operation Merge(K1,K2) to be well-defined, the result must be independent of representatives. ... This is exactly another congruence requirement. Composability is not automatic from quotient existence. ... If Merge(H1,H2) not-equiv Merge(H1',H2'), then Merge does not descend to the
b_rows_sample.statement: Proves Composability of Merge over the quotient is a distinct congruence requirement (representative-independence: equivalent inputs must produce equivalent Merge outputs), not automatic from mere quotient existence; if it fails, Merge simply does not descend to a well-defined K* x K* -> K* operation, requiring one of 5 named remedies (a richer K, additional external context, a restricted Merge domain, a partial operation, or a different semantic interpretation).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Yes. The missing part of **Step 272A** is the actual derivation of \(\Sigma\). The earlier 272A established the operation universe and the requirement that \(\Sigma\) be derived by **distinguishability**, but it stopped before performing the minimality proof.
a_rows_sample.statement: States this document is the formal completion of the earlier Step 272A (S1799, which established the operation universe O_sem and required that Sigma be derived by distinguishability) rather than a replacement for the separately-commissioned Step 272 itself.

a_rows_sample.anchor: $$\sigma_1 \equiv_E \sigma_2 \iff \forall o\in O_E,\forall x\in X_o: Obs_o(\sigma_1,x)=Obs_o(\sigma_2,x)$$ ... If there exists a mandatory epistemic operation for which two states produce different valid results, those states cannot be collapsed into one epistemic state.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the epistemic minimality criterion: two candidate epistemic states are indistinguishable with respect to a mandatory epistemic operation set iff every operation in that set produces the same observable result for both states across all valid inputs; if some mandatory operation distinguishes them, they cannot be collapsed into one state.

type_signature.domain: pair of epistemic states x mandatory operation set

a_rows_sample.anchor: $$\boxed{Unknown\ required}$$ ... Unknown does not mean false. $$Unknown(p) \neq Refuted(p)$$ Nor does it mean that no observation exists. An observation may exist while remaining insufficient to establish the proposition.
a_rows_sample.statement: Derives Unknown as a required epistemic distinction (there is no sufficient epistemic basis to classify p as supported or refuted, distinguishable via Assess), and clarifies Unknown does not mean false, nor does it mean no observation exists — an observation may exist while remaining insufficient.

a_rows_sample.anchor: $$E^+ \models p$$ and $$E^- \models \neg p$$ Then both support and refutation are simultaneously present. ... $$\boxed{Conflict\ required}$$ This is a mathematical necessity under the mandatory operation set.
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues Conflict is a mathematically necessary fourth epistemic state: when independently qualified evidence sets simultaneously support p (E+ |= p) and refute p (E- |= not-p), a three-state model {Unknown,Supported,Refuted} would have to arbitrarily choose one, losing information relevant to DetectContradiction and Resolve; hence a distinct Conflict state is required.

a_rows_sample.anchor: $$\boxed{Missingness\ is\ required\ information}$$ but: $$\boxed{Missingness\ need\ not\ be\ a\ value\ of\ the\ epistemic\ status}$$ This is precisely where the earlier formulations risked overloading Sigma.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Missing (no observation obtained) from Unknown (observation obtained but insufficient) as causally different histories relevant to data quality, evidence qualification, and audit, but concludes Missingness need not be a top-level value of the epistemic status Sigma itself -- it can be represented at the evidence/observation layer instead, correcting a risk of Sigma overload in earlier formulations.

a_rows_sample.anchor:

otin \Sigma}$$ It belongs to lifecycle/history semantics. This establishes the required separation: $$EpistemicState 
eq LifecycleState$$ ... $$ oxed{EpistemicState 
eq GovernanceState}$$ ... $$Authorized 
otin \Sigma$$ and $$Approved 
otin \Sigma$$
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes three orthogonal dimension separations: Supersession is a lifecycle/history relation, not an epistemic status (EpistemicState != LifecycleState); Authorization/Approval belong to a governance model, not the epistemic status (EpistemicState != GovernanceState); Contested and Resolution are process/workflow states derivable from Conflict+Assessment+Authority/Context rather than primitive Sigma values; Validity (Current/Stale/Expired) is temporal/contextual semantics, not epistemic status.

a_rows_sample.anchor: $$\boxed{\Sigma_0 = \{Unknown, Supported, Refuted, Conflict\}}$$ ... $$\Sigma_0(p) = (S(p),R(p))$$ produces four states ... $$\boxed{\Sigma_0 \cong \{0,1\}^2}$$
a_rows_sample.statement: Constructs Sigma_0 formally as the pair (S(p), R(p)) of binary support-qualified and refutation-qualified indicators, giving the isomorphism Sigma_0 ≅ {0,1}^2 with (0,0)=Unknown, (1,0)=Supported, (0,1)=Refuted, (1,1)=Conflict — a mathematical construction rather than a mere four-label proposal.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose we remove one state. ### Remove Unknown ... Invalid. ### Remove Supported ... Invalid. ### Remove Refuted ... Invalid. ### Remove Conflict ... Invalid. Therefore: $$\boxed{|\Sigma_0|\geq4}$$ ... $$\boxed{|\Sigma_0|=4}$$
a_rows_sample.statement: Proves minimality of the four-state structure by exhaustive deletion: removing any one of Unknown/Supported/Refuted/Conflict leaves some (S,R) combination unrepresentable, which breaks a mandatory operation's output (e.g. removing Conflict destroys DetectContradiction's output for the (1,1) case). Concludes |Sigma_0| >= 4 is forced and, since four states are sufficient, |Sigma_0| = 4 exactly.

a_rows_sample.anchor: $$\boxed{Supported \equiv QualifiedSupport > 0}$$ ... $$\Sigma_0$$ is an epistemic assessment structure, not a truth-value algebra. ... $$\boxed{Uncertainty \notin \Sigma_0}$$ ... $$\boxed{\Sigma_0\ does\ not\ require\ probability}$$ Do not introduce probability merely because uncertainty exists.
a_rows_sample.statement: Three qualifications on the derived structure: (1) Supported/Refuted are not truth values (Supported does not mean p=True); they mean QualifiedSupport/QualifiedRefutation exceed zero under some policy-dependent assessment. (2) Uncertainty/confidence does not need to be a fifth primitive Sigma value -- two Supported assertions can differ in confidence without requiring different epistemic categories, represented instead via an associated Assessment/Uncertainty function. (3) No probability space is required or implied by any of the four states; the methodological rule stated is 'do not introduce probability merely because uncertainty exists.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: $$State(p) = (\Sigma_E(p), \Lambda(p), \Gamma(p), Context(p))$$ rather than one overloaded status enum. This is a major result of the derivation. ... $$\boxed{\Sigma \perp \Lambda \perp \Gamma}$$ conceptually, even though operations may use all three. Here perp means distinct semantic dimensions, not statistical independence.
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes the overall knowledge-object state as a 4-tuple State(p) = (Sigma_E(p), Lambda(p), Gamma(p), Context(p)) -- epistemic, lifecycle, governance, context -- rather than one overloaded status enum, described as a major result. States Sigma perp Lambda perp Gamma, explicitly clarifying that perp here denotes distinct semantic dimensions (an architectural/ontological claim), not statistical independence (a measurement claim) -- a terminology caution against conflating the two senses of 'independent'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: $$\sigma_1\sqcup\sigma_2 = (s_1\lor s_2,\ r_1\lor r_2)$$ ... $$Supported\sqcup Refuted=Conflict$$ ... $$Conflict\sqcup anything=Conflict$$ ... this is a derived candidate algebra, not yet proof that all KnowledgeOS merge semantics must use it.
a_rows_sample.statement: Derives a join-semilattice merge operation over Sigma_0: sigma1 ⊔ sigma2 = (s1 OR s2, r1 OR r2), giving Unknown⊔Supported=Supported, Supported⊔Refuted=Conflict, Conflict⊔anything=Conflict, making Conflict the top element and Unknown the bottom of the {0,1}^2 lattice. a_rows_sample.statement: ATTACK 4 lands: Conflict can be entirely computed as the derived predicate S(x) AND R(x), requiring no storage beyond the two primitives (S,R). a_rows_sample.statement: ATTACK 6 lands as a boundary obligation: three distinct situations (never asked; asked with no evidence obtained; evidence obtained but insufficient) all collapse to Unknown=(0,0) in Sigma_0. a_rows_sample.anchor: ATTACK 9 — Is OR-MERGE mandated, or merely convenient? *** THE DECISIVE ONE *** ... If Sigma is STORED and merged with OR: state stays (1,1) (Conflict) FOREVER — OR is monotone, so no merge can ever clear the R bit. If Sigma is DERIVED from the evidence set: state correctly becomes Supported. **LANDS — and it decides D-4.** OR-merge is correct ONLY IF Sigma is DERIVED from the evidence set. A STORED Sigma under OR-merge cannot recover from Retract, contradicting 272B's own operation set.
a_rows_sample.statement: ATTACK 9 (marked 'THE DECISIVE ONE') lands and directly resolves decision D-4 (is Sigma stored or derived?): OR-based merge (sigma1 ⊔ sigma2 = (s1∨s2, r1∨r2)) is monotone, so if Sigma is stored as accumulated state, a Refute-then-Retract sequence (evidence e1=Support, e2=Refute reaching Conflict, then Retract(e2)) leaves the stored value permanently at Conflict since OR can never clear a bit -- yet Step 272B's own operation set includes Retract, and correctly recomputing Sigma from the current evidence set after Retract gives Supported, not Conflict. Conclusion: Sigma must be DERIVED (recomputed from the live evidence set) rather than stored/accumulated, or the theory contradicts its own Retract operation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: DECISIVE: strength is POLICY-RELATIVE; (S,R) is POLICY-INVARIANT. two supporting items, bar=2 -> "Moderate"; bar=3 -> "Weak" the same evidence, a different policy, a different grade. the POLARITY of that evidence does not move when the bar moves. b_rows_sample.statement: TEST 3, described as decisive: strength is policy-relative (the same underlying evidence produces a different grade under a different sufficiency-bar policy), whereas (S,R) polarity is policy-invariant (the polarity of the evidence itself does not change when the policy bar changes). Since a component whose value changes with policy cannot belong inside a policy-independent Sigma (citing the corpus's own boxed rule that Policy is NOT-IN Identity(K), Step 271 s271.3), the graded strength scale must live outside Sigma, in the assessment layer.

MT-5 also stands: no empirical relational structure was ever given for the scale, so even its ORDINALITY is assumed rather than established. NOTE, honestly: not every rule flips
b_rows_sample.statement: TEST 4 exhaustively re-establishes the corpus's own earlier finding MT-3 (that an ordinal scale under an arbitrary order-preserving re-encoding can flip the verdict of a mean/threshold decision rule) not via a single hand-picked example but via exhaustive search over three order-preserving encodings, all portfolio sizes 1-3, and all integer thresholds 1-7, finding multiple flipping (portfolio, threshold) pairs. Also reaffirms first-order finding MT-5: the strength scale's ordinality itself is assumed, never established via an empirical relational structure. Explicitly notes not every decision rule flips (min/max/median are invariant), so meaningfulness must be checked per-rule, not declared uniformly wrong.

b_rows_sample.anchor: THEREFORE: Sigma = P({Support, Refute}) policy-INVARIANT, derived from evidence ; Strength = f(evidence, policy) policy-RELATIVE, an ASSESSMENT output ... They are neither competing definitions of Sigma nor orthogonal dimensions. Step 275 and Step 272B answer DIFFERENT questions, and the contradiction dissolves once Assessment is separated from Sigma
b_rows_sample.statement: Final resolution of the Step 275 vs Step 272B tension: adjudicating five hypotheses about the graded strength scale S's relationship to Sigma -- (a) part of Sigma: NO, policy-relative while Sigma is not; (b) orthogonal: NO, refuted by nesting (Test 1); (c) derivable: YES, strength=f(evidence,policy) over the same evidence set Sigma derives from; (d) policy-dependent: YES, and this is precisely why it is excluded from Sigma; (e) obsolete: NO, three operations (Qualify, Assess, Compare) need it. Concludes Sigma is the coarsest policy-invariant abstraction of the evidence set, while Strength is a policy-relative refinement of that same evidence set produced by the Assessment layer -- Step 275 and Step 272B are answering different questions, not contradicting each other, once Assessment is properly separated from Sigma (per s271.10-11's Assessment != Truth, Assessment != Inference, and 272A.7).

a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes five coexisting gap classes: G1 Semantic (software loses domain meaning), G2 Governance (authority/responsibility ambiguous), G3 Temporal (historical state not reconstructable), G4 Epistemic (evidence/uncertainty/assumptions lost), G5 Assurance (behavior may be correct but insufficiently evidenced).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Implementation = Present but Assurance = Weak. This is not necessarily an implementation gap. It is an: Assurance Gap

a_rows_sample.anchor: ArchitectureGap != ImplementationGap != VerificationGap
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Architecture gap (design itself lacks the mechanism), Implementation gap (mechanism specified but code does not implement it correctly), and Verification gap (implementation appears correct but evidence is insufficient) as three non-identical gap types.

a_rows_sample.anchor: TechnicalCapability=Present while GovernanceCapability=Missing ... Ownerless Invariants ... Shared responsibility must not mean undefined responsibility
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies a governance gap pattern where a technical mechanism (AI->Assessment->Approval) works but nobody has defined who is authorized to approve, so TechnicalCapability=Present while GovernanceCapability=Missing; introduces the 'ownerless invariant' search (Owner(I)=empty set, dangerous because nobody maintains it) and its converse, the 'shared ownership' problem, where undivided shared responsibility (Owner(I)={A,B,C}) risks each team assuming another enforces the invariant -- boxed as 'shared responsibility must not mean undefined responsibility'.

a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a semantic-loss function for a context-to-context contract L(C)=InformationBefore(C)-InformationAfter(C), refined to Loss(C) as the set of critical properties absent after transformation; worked example: an Assessment=(score,uncertainty,modelVersion,evidenceRef) contract sending only {score} loses uncertainty/modelVersion/evidenceRef, a Critical Semantic Gap if downstream governance requires them.
